If you want to move hosting to GoDaddy but keep the domain registration where it is, you usually just change the domain’s DNS/nameservers to point to GoDaddy.

Steps:
1. Log in to the current domain registrar (CrazyDomains).
2. Find the domain’s DNS or Nameserver settings.
3. Replace the existing nameservers with the ones GoDaddy gives you, or switch the domain’s A record to the new GoDaddy server IP.
4. Save changes and wait for DNS propagation, which can take a few hours to 48 hours.

If you only change hosting, the domain itself can stay unchanged.  
If you want, I can help you find the exact GoDaddy nameservers or explain whether to change nameservers vs A record.

Yes—Google Analytics can show combined stats for multiple sites, but not by putting all sites into one property the way you described.

What to do:
- Create one GA account
- Create one property
- Create a separate profile/view for each site
- Create one additional “All Web Site Data” view that includes all your sites

For the combined view, use filters so it includes traffic from all 40 domains. For each site-specific view, filter to only that domain.

Tracking code:
- Use the same GA tracking ID on all sites if you want them rolled up into the same property
- No special tracking code is needed

Note: In modern Google Analytics, “profiles” are now called “views.”

Yes—there isn’t a built-in “combine all properties” view in classic Google Analytics.

Best options:

- **Universal Analytics / same tracking code across sites**: If available in your account, you can create a new property/profile and use one tracking setup across multiple domains.
- **Cross-domain tracking**: For classic GA, this is the usual way to track multiple domains together.
- **Third-party analytics/log tools**: Some tools can aggregate stats from multiple sites or server logs.
- **For server capacity**: Use actual server monitoring tools (e.g., `top`, Task Manager, or similar) rather than GA real-time users.

If you want, I can also explain how to set up cross-domain tracking or how to approximate combined totals manually.

Google likely found those pages through normal discovery signals, even if you didn’t manually link them from a visible page. Common ways include:

- Internal links in your site’s HTML, XML sitemap, or navigation
- A sitemap submitted in Google Search Console
- External mentions/links from other sites, social posts, or feeds
- URL patterns discovered from crawling similar pages on your site
- “Ping”/publication notifications from your CMS or sitemap updates

If the pages were truly unlinked, Google may still have found them via your sitemap, server logs, or another source that exposed the URL. To make discovery faster, add them to an XML sitemap, link them from an already crawled page, and request indexing in Search Console.

If you’re changing hosting companies, the key point is that jQuery itself won’t be affected by the host. jQuery runs in the browser, so any normal web host can serve the files and the script will work.

What matters is whether the host supports your server-side needs, such as:
- PHP, Python, Ruby, Node.js, etc.
- databases like MySQL
- any special permissions or cron jobs you need

So when comparing hosts, focus on:
- uptime and speed
- storage/bandwidth
- support for your backend stack
- backup/security features

If you only need a static site plus jQuery, almost any host will do.

Changing web hosting usually does not affect SEO rankings by itself. Search engines rank your pages based on content, relevance, and user experience, not the hosting company.

The main risk is during the move:
- downtime
- broken links
- slow loading after migration

If you keep the site available and the new host performs well, your rankings should be fine. Very slow hosting can hurt SEO indirectly, but only if it seriously affects page speed. A smooth, low-downtime migration is ideal.

Google can discover new pages even without links. Common ways include:

- The domain was found via DNS, WHOIS, or registrar data.
- Your server may have been reachable from other known pages or hosts.
- Google may have crawled the IP address or guessed common URLs.
- If you had any sitemap, robots.txt, or analytics/request traffic, that can help discovery too.

In the resolved thread context, the key idea is: yes, search engines can use registrar/WHOIS-related information and other signals to find newly registered domains. So “unlinked” doesn’t mean “undiscoverable.”

Google likely didn’t find those pages from your new content. Common sources are:

- Old URLs still present in the database or theme/plugin settings
- Cached references in sitemap, feeds, menus, widgets, or redirects
- Internal links in content you deleted but that still exist in revision tables or serialized data
- External backlinks or old crawl data Google already had

Best check:
1. Search your files and database for the old domain/URLs.
2. Inspect sitemap and robots.txt.
3. Check for redirects and leftover plugin/theme settings.
4. Remember WordPress often stores URLs in serialized data, so use a safe search tool.

If you want, I can give you a step-by-step checklist for WordPress.

The most objective way is to use a rank-checking tool that queries the search engine from a neutral location and reports your position for specific keywords.

Quick manual checks:
- To see if you’re indexed: search for your domain name or use `site:yourdomain.com`.
- To check ranking: search the keywords you care about and note where your page appears.

Keep in mind:
- Rankings vary by location, device, language, and personalization.
- So don’t rely on just one browser or your own search history.

For the most accurate repeatable result, use:
- Google Search Console for visibility/click data
- A third-party rank tracker for keyword positions

Yes, that can happen.

A sitemap is only a list of URLs you want Google to discover; it is not a list of everything Google can find or index. Google may index URLs that are:

- linked from other pages
- found in old sitemaps
- discovered through external links
- generated by parameters, redirects, or canonical variations

So Google can have more indexed URLs than are in your current sitemap if those URLs were discovered elsewhere.

Also, sitemap submission does not guarantee indexing. Google decides what to crawl and keep indexed based on quality, duplication, canonical tags, internal links, and other signals.

To check ranking objectively, don’t rely on a logged-in/browser personalized search result.

Use one of these:
- Google Search Console: shows average position, impressions, clicks, and queries.
- Incognito/private window, with location/language set consistently.
- Rank trackers/tools like SEMrush, Ahrefs, AccuRanker, etc.

Important: rankings can vary by country, device, time, and personalization, so a sudden “drop” may just be a different search context. If many keywords vanish, check Search Console for manual actions or algorithmic issues, and verify whether Google indexed your pages.

This is normal. A sitemap is only a list of URLs you’re telling Google about; it is not a count of what Google has indexed.

Google can index URLs from other sources too, such as:
- internal links
- external backlinks
- old URLs it already knew about
- redirected or canonicalized variants

Also, Google may not index every URL in the sitemap. Some may be crawled but excluded, not yet processed, or considered duplicate/low value.

So Google having more indexed URLs than your sitemap contains usually means it found additional URLs elsewhere, and the sitemap is only advisory.

Google can index URLs that are not in your sitemap. A sitemap is only a discovery hint, not a complete list of indexed pages.

Common reasons Google has more indexed URLs than your sitemap:
- URLs linked internally or externally
- old URLs still in the index
- parameterized/duplicate URLs
- canonical issues
- pages discovered through feeds, XML sitemaps, or redirects

If your sitemap is large and changes daily, split it into multiple sitemaps and use a sitemap index. Organize them by site section or category. This makes updates easier and can help Google process them more efficiently.

You generally can’t “set” a dynamic host URL on your router to make it static. If your public IP changes, the usual solution is Dynamic DNS (DDNS): a service or client updates your DNS record automatically whenever your ISP changes your IP.

Options:
- Ask your ISP for a static IP
- Use a DDNS provider
- Manually update DNS when the IP changes (not ideal)

If you use DDNS, keep TTL low enough to reduce stale records, but not so low that it hurts performance. If this is for a website, a normal web host is often simpler and more reliable than hosting from home.

“Expiration headers” means telling the browser how long it can cache static files like CSS, JS, and images.

Set cache headers on the web server, not in HTML. Examples:

Apache (.htaccess):
```apache
<IfModule mod_expires.c>
  ExpiresActive On
  ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType image/png "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/gif "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/webp "access plus 1 year"
</IfModule>
```

Nginx:
```nginx
location ~* \.(css|js|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp)$ {
  expires 30d;
  add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=2592000";
}
```

You can also use `Cache-Control: max-age=...`.

If you mean the host in your sitemap URLs, yes—you can generate it dynamically from the current request/server config instead of hardcoding `127.0.0.1`.

Best practice:
- Use the configured base URL or request host
- Don’t hardcode environment-specific values
- Generate the full `<loc>` at runtime

Example idea:
- `https://` + current host + path

If you mean the XML `<changefreq>` value, you can generate it dynamically too, but it’s usually better to leave it out unless you’re sure it adds value. Search engines often don’t rely on it much.

Use Apache mod_expires. It’s simpler than setting headers per folder/file type.

Example:

ExpiresActive On
ExpiresDefault "access plus 24 hours"
ExpiresByType image/jpg "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType image/png "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType image/gif "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType text/javascript "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 month"

Put this in your Apache config or .htaccess for CSS, JS, and images. Make sure mod_expires is enabled. If you also use mod_headers, avoid conflicting Cache-Control/Expires rules.

If you want to change the host used for a site, the simplest approach is to edit your local hosts file rather than trying to rewrite the HTTP Host header in the browser.

That lets you map the domain name to the server’s IP on your machine, so requests still use the correct hostname while resolving to the new address. It also works beyond just GET requests and applies to other protocols too.

In short: update your hosts file with the domain → IP mapping, then browse normally using the domain name.

To set expiration headers for CSS, JS, and images, configure your web server or CDN to send cache headers like:

- `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, public`  
- optionally `Expires: <future date>`

Example idea: for static assets, use a long max-age, e.g. 1 year.

If you’re using Apache, Nginx, or a CDN, set this in their config rather than in the files themselves.

Note: if your goal is to stop indexing non-HTML files, use `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` or `robots.txt`; that’s separate from expiration/caching headers.

If you only need to fix it for development and can edit the pages, the simplest workaround is to change the internal links to include the full URL, e.g. `http://example.com/en/home/` instead of `/en/home/`.

That forces the browser to go directly to the correct page and avoids the bad relative path.

If the links are generated by templates or CMS, update the base path or link target there. If you can’t change the source HTML, then you’d need a server-side redirect or a client-side script to intercept clicks.

Self-hosted analytics like Urchin can be useful if you need:

- Runs on your own servers, so you keep data in-house
- Works for intranets/private sites
- Can process historical server logs
- Robot/spider reports
- Status and error code reports, like 404s
- Individual visitor history drilldown

Those are the main advantages over Google Analytics noted in the comparison. The big downside is cost: Urchin was not cheap, listed around US$9,995.

This usually happens when the form submit isn’t tracked as a proper on-site event, so Analytics later attributes the conversion to the last referrer, like Facebook or accounts.google.com.

Best fix:
- Fire a Google Analytics event when the contact form is successfully submitted.
- Create the Goal in Google Analytics based on that event, not on a page URL.

Why this helps:
- The conversion is recorded at the moment the form is completed.
- GA won’t rely on the referrer from a later page or redirect.
- It prevents misattribution to social/login sources.

If needed, also check:
- Cross-domain tracking
- Referral exclusion / unwanted referral settings
- UTMs on paid/social campaigns

This usually happens because Google Analytics is seeing the conversion on a referral from another site, not as your own traffic.

To prevent misattribution to Facebook or `accounts.google.com`:

- Add your own domain and trusted payment/auth domains to the **Referral Exclusion List** in GA.
- Make sure the GA tag is installed correctly on **all pages**, especially the goal/thank-you page.
- If you use Facebook login or Google sign-in, keep their domains excluded so the session doesn’t restart as a referral.
- In GA4, also check **cross-domain measurement** if the journey spans multiple domains.

Also, as in the resolved thread, ensure the tracking script is placed correctly in the page, ideally inside `<head>` or just before `</body>`, not outside the HTML document.

In Google Analytics goal setup, use only the path, not the domain or subdomain. So if the conversion page is:

/conversions/

enter just that as the goal URL.

If you’re seeing referrals from Facebook or accounts.google.com on goal conversions, that usually means the traffic is being attributed to the last non-direct source before the conversion. To reduce misattribution:

- Make sure GA tracking is installed on both the main domain and all subdomains
- Use cross-domain tracking if users move between domains you own
- Exclude unwanted referrals in GA settings
- Verify auto-tagging / UTM tagging for paid campaigns

For subdomains, GA should automatically attribute the goal to the correct page path as long as tracking is consistent.

You generally should not add `http://` to internal links unless the page is actually on another domain or protocol.

For internal links, use relative URLs or root-relative URLs like:

- `/about`
- `/products/item-1`

Why:
- Keeps links portable if your domain changes
- Avoids mixed-content issues when on HTTPS
- Helps crawlers and browsers treat them as internal

If you meant “make search engines crawl internal pages faster,” adding `http://` won’t help. Better to:
- keep the pages linked normally
- include them in your sitemap
- make sure the pages are generated/cached ahead of time

If you want, I can also explain when absolute URLs are preferable.

Yes—don’t do that. Google AdSense prohibits encouraging users to click ads directly or indirectly.

Phrases like:
- “click the ads”
- “support us”
- “check out our sponsors”
- “visit these links”

can all be considered encouraging clicks and may violate the policy.

Safer approach:
- Keep ads clearly separate from your own content
- Don’t add arrows, labels, or calls to action pointing at ads
- Use neutral placement and standard ad units

If you want, I can help you phrase a policy-safe “Sponsored” section for your site.

`http://` is not the cause of `nofollow`, and `.htaccess` cannot add `rel="nofollow"` to links. `nofollow` is usually coming from: - your CMS/theme/plugin/module - the HTML template - a script that renders links - a manual edit in the content What to do: 1. View page source and search for `rel="nofollow"`. 2. Check your CMS settings, theme, and plugins/extensions. 3. Make sure your internal links use normal HTML like: `Link` 4. Set one canonical version of the site with 301 redirects for `www/non-www` and `index.html`. If you want, paste your `.htaccess` and I can check it.

If your AdSense ads aren’t showing on your website, check these first:

- Is your AdSense account approved, under review, or disabled?
- Did you paste the ad code exactly as provided?
- Is JavaScript enabled, and are you using an ad blocker?
- Are you showing more than 3 ad units on a page?
- Is your site content AdSense-friendly and not restricted?
- Can Google crawl your site properly? Check Search Console/Webmaster Tools for crawl errors.

Also, some website builders can interfere with ad placement, so the platform may matter.

If you want, tell me what website creator you’re using and I can help narrow it down.

If you suspect invalid-click “bombing,” the key is to detect and limit it, not to figure out the attacker’s tool.

What to do:
- Replace AdSense temporarily with a test ad/script that logs IP, timestamp, user agent, referrer, and click count.
- Look for repeated clicks from the same IPs, bots, or suspicious traffic patterns.
- Report invalid clicks to Google AdSense using their invalid-clicks form.
- Consider showing ads only to trusted traffic sources, such as search-engine visitors.
- Use basic anti-bot protection, rate limiting, and server-side logging.

Also, if your AdSense account was disabled for invalid clicks, recovery is often difficult. For the future, monitor traffic closely and keep evidence of suspicious behavior.

Hyphens are not bad by themselves. Search engines can index hyphenated domains normally.

That said, the resolved thread suggests that domains with multiple hyphens may not get the same “exact match” keyword benefit as a cleaner, non-hyphenated version. So hyphens usually aren’t a penalty, but too many of them can make a domain less appealing and possibly slightly less helpful for keyword relevance.

In short:
- 1 hyphen: generally fine
- multiple hyphens: can look spammy and may reduce keyword benefit
- ranking depends much more on content, links, and site quality than the domain name

So hyphens aren’t “bad,” but fewer is usually better.

Hyphens aren’t “bad,” but they’re usually less desirable in a domain name.

Why people often avoid them:
- Harder to say and remember out loud
- More annoying to type and share
- Can look less polished or trustworthy

When hyphens can help:
- If the words are otherwise ambiguous or misleading
- To improve readability in a multi-word domain

For SEO, hyphens are generally not a major advantage anymore. For user friendliness, a clean non-hyphenated domain is usually better if you can get it.

If you want the simplest way to let people message you from your website, embed a chat widget from an IM service.

For example, the resolved case used the Google Talk chatback widget: you just paste the HTML snippet they provide into your page. Visitors can then send you messages directly while you stay logged in.

If you want a different service, look for its “chat widget,” “contact badge,” or “embed code” option.

Use an SMS gateway service that provides an HTTP/API interface. A common option is Clickatell, which can send and receive SMS from PHP and other languages.

Typical steps:
1. Sign up with an SMS gateway provider.
2. Get API credentials.
3. Call their HTTP API from your website/backend to send messages.
4. Set up an inbound SMS callback/webhook to process replies.

If you need PHP/ASP examples, I can show a basic integration pattern.

If you already have a way to send the texts, you just need:

1. A subscription/payment system to collect monthly fees  
   - PayPal’s recurring subscription/billing is a common choice.
   - You can configure it as a monthly product and automate renewals.

2. A backend to track active subscribers  
   - Store user status, payment state, and subscription dates in your DB.
   - When payment succeeds, keep the account active; when it fails/cancels, stop messages.

3. A message-sending queue or cron job  
   - Schedule messages throughout the month and trigger your SMS/email API.

Also make cancellation very easy for users to avoid payment disputes.

To send messages from your website, use an SMS gateway API.

The earlier thread suggests searching for “International SMS Gateway.” Twilio was mentioned as very developer-friendly, and cdyne’s SMS service was also recommended.

Typical flow:
1. Users send SMS to your gateway number.
2. The gateway posts incoming messages to your ASP.NET server via webhook/API.
3. You store/display votes.
4. Your site triggers an API call to send a reply SMS to the winner.

If you want, I can help outline the ASP.NET webhook and send-message API flow.

To add SMS to your website, use an SMS gateway API.

Search for: “International SMS Gateway” or “SMS API”. These services let you:
- receive inbound texts via a webhook to your web server
- send outbound texts from your app

Twilio is one option and is very developer-friendly, but if you need international coverage, contact them directly to ask about Australia support and references. Another provider mentioned is cdyne’s SMS service.

Typical flow:
1. User texts your assigned number
2. Provider posts the message to your backend
3. You store/update vote results
4. Your site triggers an outbound SMS to the winner

If you want, I can suggest current international SMS API providers for ASP.NET.

You generally should not try to make Google index your AJAX search result pages.

Instead:
- Create an XML sitemap for your real content pages.
- Submit it to Google.
- Keep it updated automatically.

Google can index your actual pages directly, without crawling your internal search results. Making search result pages crawlable can create an almost infinite number of URLs, waste crawl budget, and cause stale or low-value pages to be indexed.

If you need the AJAX results accessible to users and bots, expose the underlying content pages with normal, crawlable URLs, not site-search result pages.

For SEO, the key issue is whether the snapshot page shows the same main content as the user-facing page.

Different tags like `h1`, `h2`, or layout differences are usually fine if the text/content is equivalent. Google can render AJAX apps, but for crawlable snapshots you should avoid showing substantially different content, links, or keywords than users see.

So:
- Same content = generally OK
- Different structure/tags = usually OK
- Different meaning/content = risky, could be seen as cloaking

Best practice: make the snapshot page as close as possible to the rendered user page, especially for visible text and links.

Google’s indexing has changed since that older thread. In many cases, Google can now crawl and render AJAX/JavaScript content directly, so the old “AJAX crawling” scheme is largely obsolete.

For your search result pages, the key points are:

- Make sure the page has a unique, crawlable URL for each result set.
- Ensure important content is present in the rendered HTML or can be rendered by Googlebot.
- Don’t rely on “Submit to index” in Search Console; it may not do anything for some AJAX/JS URLs.
- Use Fetch/Inspect URL to verify Google can see the rendered content.
- Check that the page isn’t blocked by robots.txt, noindex, or requiring user interaction to load content.

If you want, I can help you troubleshoot a specific AJAX search URL pattern.

If the “bots” are hitting a PHP script directly, robots.txt won’t help much. Don’t rely on crawl-delay either.

Best fix:
- Make the script inaccessible unless it’s included by your own code.
- Define a constant in the main page, then `include` the script.
- In the script, check for that constant; if missing, return 403 or blank output.

Example idea:
- main page: define a constant, then include the PHP file
- script: `if (!defined('MY_APP')) exit;`

Also, use `include` with a local file path, not `file_get_contents()` or a URL.

If possible, move the script outside the web root so it can’t be requested directly.

Yes — bots can absolutely be part of abuse, especially if they’re POSTing forms.

Common defenses:
- Hidden honeypot field: humans won’t fill it, bots often will.
- CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha).
- Simple challenge question, e.g. “What is 5 + 3?”
- CSRF-style token tied to the session/form and verified on submit.
- Rate limiting: per IP, account, or device; block bursts.
- IP reputation / temporary bans for repeated abuse.
- JavaScript-generated token or timestamp can help, but don’t rely on it alone; determined bots can run JS.
- Spam filtering services like Akismet for user-generated content.

Best practice is to combine several layers: token + honeypot + rate limiting + CAPTCHA for suspicious traffic.

Use user-agent detection, not IP addresses.

Search engine bots do not have a stable, complete IP list you can rely on, and their IPs change frequently. The usual approach is:

- Check the HTTP User-Agent string for known bots
- Optionally verify by reverse DNS / forward DNS for major bots if you need stronger validation
- Maintain your own deny/allow list of known bot user agents

For a “users online” counter, also consider that:
- Some bots spoof user agents
- Some legitimate users may have privacy tools that make detection less reliable

So the practical answer is: there is no always-up-to-date master list of all bot IPs, and filtering by user agent is the standard solution.

This can happen because Google Analytics treats single-page visits differently.

- Avg Time on Page includes time spent before the next tracked pageview or exit.
- Avg Visit Duration / Avg Time on Site counts bounces as 0 seconds.

So if many users land on one page, read it, and leave, that page can show a high Avg Time on Page, while the site/session average stays low because those visits are counted as 0.

In short: lots of bounces can make Avg Time on Page larger than Avg Visit Duration.

In Google Analytics, you can’t really “hide all traffic” from the chart, but you can exclude specific rows/pages from being counted in the selected view.

Use a filter:

1. Go to Google Analytics.
2. Select the correct View.
3. Click Admin.
4. Under View, choose Filters.
5. Click New Filter.
6. Choose Custom.
7. Filter by:
   - Page Title, if the page has a unique title, or
   - Request URI / Page URL, if you want to match part of the URL.
8. Save.

If your goal is to remove one page from “all traffic,” filtering by the page URL or title is usually the cleanest approach.

Yes — instead of using **Plot Rows**, use the **Motion Charts** view.

Steps:
1. Go to **Traffic Sources → Sources → Referrals**.
2. Make sure the referrers you want are all on the same page.
3. Click the **Motion Charts** icon (three black dots at top right of the graph).
4. In the graph, switch the metric on the left to **Visits**.
5. Click the **line chart** tab/icon.
6. Use the checkboxes to select only the referrer domains you want.

This avoids the big **“all traffic”** line and lets you compare just the domains you care about.

Yes—this can happen, and it’s usually not an error.

In Google Analytics, **Avg. Time on Page** can be larger than **Avg. Visit Duration** because they’re calculated differently:

- **Avg. Visit Duration** = time between the first and last tracked interaction in a session.
- **Avg. Time on Page** = time spent on a specific page, based on hits/events.

A session with only one pageview often shows **0:00:00 visit duration**, even if the person stayed on that page for a while, because GA needs another hit to measure the time. So a lot of 0-second visits usually means the user left before another tracked interaction occurred, not necessarily robots.

Yes — this can happen because the two metrics are calculated differently.

Avg. Time on Page looks at how long users stayed on that page before going to another page on your site. It excludes exits and single-page visits.

Avg. Visit Duration is based on the total time between the first and last pageview in a visit. The last pageview can’t be fully timed, so this metric is often understated.

So if you want to know how long users typically spent on that specific page before moving on, use Avg. Time on Page.

Those 404s are most likely caused by a bad relative link on your site, not by Google or WordPress itself.

In the resolved case, the culprit was a banner image/link in the page source:

`<a href="_#">`

Because it’s a relative URL, Google resolves it as `yourdomain.com/_`, which returns 404. If that link appears on many pages, Webmaster Tools will report lots of 404s.

What to do:
- View your page source and search for `href="_#"` or just `href="_`
- Check widgets, header banners, ads, or custom HTML
- Fix the link to a valid URL or remove it

Once corrected, Google will stop finding those `/_` URLs.

This is usually normal. Googlebot often requests random, non-existent URLs like `tyuiabmog.html` to verify your site’s 404 behavior and confirm that missing pages return a real 404 status code.

If Google Webmaster Tools shows many 404s:
- Check that your server returns HTTP 404, not 200, for missing pages.
- Make sure your custom 404 page is user-friendly but still sends a 404 status.
- Review linked pages, old URLs, or bad backlinks if the same missing URL is being hit repeatedly.

A few random 404s are expected and not a problem.

For discontinued product pages, use a 410 Gone if the page is permanently removed so search engines know it’s gone faster than with a 404. If you keep the page, leave it live with a clear “discontinued” message and helpful links to similar products, your homepage, sitemap, and contact page.

If the item is seasonal or may return, don’t use 410/404. Keep the page indexed, mark it as temporarily unavailable, and consider a “notify me when back in stock” option.

Google Webmaster Tools reporting 170 “Not found (404)” errors usually means Google has found URLs on your site that no longer exist.

What to do:
1. Check the listed URLs and make sure they are truly fixed.
2. If a page moved, set up a 301 redirect to the correct URL.
3. If the page should not exist, return a proper 404 or 410.
4. Update internal links and sitemap so they point to valid pages.
5. In Search Console, mark the errors as fixed after you’ve corrected them.

If Google sees those broken URLs again, it will report them again. If not, they’ll eventually drop out of the report.

This warning usually means Google can’t validate the Product/Offer markup against visible page content.

Common causes:
- The page doesn’t show the same price, availability, or review data that’s in structured data.
- The marked-up item isn’t the main focus of the page.
- Required properties are missing in the Product/Offer schema.
- Offer is duplicated or conflicting.

For Product rich results, make sure your markup includes at least one of:
- price
- availability
- review / aggregateRating

For SEO, use dashes only when they improve readability for separate words, e.g. `example-keyword.com`. Avoid using them to “break up” one word. Short, clear, brandable domains without dashes are generally better.

Usually, avoid dashes if you can. A no-dash domain is easier to say, type, remember, and share.

If the double letters make it look awkward, a dash is acceptable, but it can also be more error-prone: people may forget it or assume the non-dash version.

Best practice:
- Prefer the cleanest non-dash version
- If possible, register both versions
- Redirect one to the other

That way you protect the name and avoid losing traffic to typos.

Including dashes in a domain name usually doesn’t help SEO. It’s mainly a branding/protection choice.

Search engines generally don’t give a ranking boost just because a domain has hyphens. A dash can make the words easier for people to read, but it’s not a meaningful SEO advantage. The only rare exception is when the words could be misread together, but even then the benefit is small.

If you already have a non-dashed domain, registering the dashed version and redirecting it is mostly useful to protect your brand and catch typos, not to improve rankings.

- robots.txt and meta tags to make sure you’re not blocking crawling/indexing
- recent site changes, redirects, or noindex tags
- whether the content still follows Google’s quality guidelines

If you think it’s a penalty, fix any guideline violations and then submit a reconsideration request in Search Console. Also note that Google may take time to re-crawl and restore rankings.

If your blog has suddenly dropped from page 1, the most likely causes are:

- technical SEO issues,

Given the context, your site may be violating AdSense/Google quality policies if it has excessive ads, popups, or unsafe scripts. That can also hurt search rankings.

What to do:

2. Review recent changes to content, ads, theme, and redirects.
3. Remove intrusive ads/popups and any suspicious scripts.
4. Improve original content and page speed.
5. Submit a reconsideration only if you find a manual action.

A sudden ranking drop is usually one of these:

- competitors gained stronger links or improved SEO
- you lost quality backlinks
- Google made a small algorithm tweak that favored others or penalized a weakness
- natural ranking fluctuation

To diagnose it:
1. Check whether the sites that outranked you recently changed or are new.
2. Review your backlink profile for lost or devalued links.
3. Look for any recent site changes and revert them if possible.
4. Verify you’re not affected by an algorithm update or manual issue.
5. Don’t panic or make big changes immediately.

If your content is still solid, wait a bit and keep earning quality links. Rankings often bounce back.

What you’re seeing is usually normal Google index/ranking fluctuation, not necessarily a penalty.

Google constantly re-crawls and re-evaluates pages, so counts and rankings can jump up or down temporarily. Resubmitting your sitemap does not “reset” rankings, but it can encourage Google to crawl pages again, which may make changes visible sooner.

Your new page, canonical tags, and 404 header could also have affected how Google interprets your site. The key point: don’t make more major changes right away. Wait a few days to see if the new state settles.

If rankings dropped right after your edits, review those changes carefully and consider rolling back only if they were likely harmful.

Google hasn’t lost your historical keyword data. The “all green / infinity” you’re seeing usually means those queries went from unmeasured or zero activity to some measurable impressions/position changes, so the percentage change is effectively infinite.

Your traffic drop can still be real if you lost rankings on a smaller set of high-volume keywords, while gaining visibility on lots of long-tail terms. Search Console/WMT can look positive overall even when total traffic falls.

What to do:
- Sort queries by loss, not gain
- Compare current period vs previous period
- Check which high-traffic keywords dropped most
- Review landing pages and ranking changes

This pattern is consistent with an algorithmic/ranking shift, not deleted history.

If your page ranks well for multi-word phrases but drops for a single phrase, it’s usually because the single term is much more competitive and has different search intent. Short keywords are often dominated by strong, older, more authoritative sites.

From the resolved thread: if the site is new, it can take time for Google to trust it. Also, even if the term is in your domain, title, and H1, that alone won’t guarantee top rankings.

Check:
- how long the page/site has been live
- competition for that exact single word
- backlinks and authority
- whether the page truly matches the intent for that query

In short: single-word rankings are harder, and delay/competition is the most likely reason.

This sounds like proxy/content theft, where Google briefly indexed the copied version. If the clone is gone, your rankings may recover, but it can take time after Google re-crawls and re-evaluates your site.

What to do:

- Submit a fresh crawl request in Google Search Console.
- Check for duplicate content or technical issues on your site.

- Update important pages so Google sees they’re original and active.

A drop in rankings for one keyword/phrase usually means Google re-evaluated relevance for that query, not necessarily your whole site.

Common causes:
- Content is not the best match for that exact phrase
- Competitors improved their pages
- On-page SEO changed: title, headings, internal links, anchor text
- Backlinks to that page lost quality or were removed
- Search intent changed, or Google prefers different page types now
- Technical issues: indexing, canonical tags, noindex, duplicate content, slow pages

Check:

2. Whether the page is still indexed
3. Recent content or site changes
4. Competitor pages ranking now

If your rankings dropped on a single phrase, it’s usually not because of meta keywords. Search engines largely ignore the meta keywords tag, so changing it won’t improve rankings.

Best practice:

- Focus on the page title, H1, headings, body content, internal links, and backlinks.
- Make sure the page matches the search intent for that phrase.
- Check for technical issues: indexation, canonicals, noindex, duplicate content, thin content, page speed, and mobile usability.

If only one phrase dropped, it may be due to competition, content relevance, or an algorithm update rather than keyword tags.

This can happen for a few reasons, and it’s not always a penalty.

If your link building just started, Google may simply be re-crawling and re-syncing its data across datacenters, so rankings can temporarily disappear or fluctuate. Also, new links can take time to be fully reflected.

What to do:
- Verify the site is still indexed with a site: search
- Set up Google Search Console/Webmaster Tools
- Check for crawl errors, manual actions, or indexing issues
- Keep monitoring for a few days to a couple of weeks

If the link building was aggressive or unnatural, that can also cause ranking drops, so make sure the links are high quality and relevant.

A common reason is that your redesign changed the URLs or site structure, so the old links now point to different addresses. For example, example.com and www.example.com are treated as different unless you redirect one to the other. The same applies if page paths changed.

Make sure:
- old URLs use 301 permanent redirects to the new URLs
- both www and non-www versions are handled consistently
- internal links and canonicals are updated

Also, Google may take time to re-evaluate links and rankings after major changes, so the link credit may not return immediately. If link building started at the same time, Google may also be re-checking the quality and relevance of those new signals.

To avoid duplicate-content SEO issues when moving to site-wide HTTPS, do this:

1. Pick one canonical version: `https://` for every page.
2. 301 redirect all `http://` URLs to the matching `https://` URLs.
3. Update internal links, sitemap, and canonical tags to HTTPS.
4. Verify the HTTPS version in Google Search Console and submit the HTTPS sitemap.
5. Keep the old HTTP URLs redirecting permanently.

If you simply enable HTTPS without redirects, Google may see both HTTP and HTTPS as duplicates. Proper 301s and canonicals usually preserve rankings and consolidate indexing.

If you’re migrating from HTTP to HTTPS, ranking loss is usually temporary while Google reindexes.

Yes, a sudden drop like this can happen on newer sites, but it’s not usually because of the 2 guest posts alone.

Common causes:

2. Coverage/report for pages dropped from the index
3. Recent backlink profile for spammy or over-optimized links
4. Whether the site is still crawlable and indexable

If the site is only 3 months old, some volatility is normal, but a near-total drop is worth investigating in Search Console first.

A ranking drop usually means Google sees the site as less relevant, less trustworthy, or less useful than before.

Common causes:

For the keywords “backlink service/backlinks service,” this niche is very competitive and sensitive to link quality.

- Resubmit your sitemap in Google Search Console
- Check for crawl errors / 404s

This is likely not a real Bingbot or Googlebot request.

Those IPs belong to Google, and the pattern matches Google’s PageSpeed service/cache proxy behavior. If Bing or Google crawls a URL that goes through that service, the request may be forwarded to your site with a Bingbot user-agent, making it look confusing in logs.

So:
- User-agent alone is not enough to trust the bot
- Whois/IP lookup shows the request came via Google infrastructure
- Most likely this is a proxy/cache fetch, not a genuine Bing crawler

To verify true bots, check reverse DNS and official verification methods for Google/Bing.

So the risk is real, but Google often ignores spammy links unless they’re extreme. Best practice is to monitor your backlink profile and disavow only if there’s a clear pattern of toxic links.

Yes, in some cases competitors can try to hurt your rankings with “negative SEO,” such as spammy backlinks or fake signals. 

That said, search engines are usually good at ignoring many low-quality links, and they often don’t penalize a site just because bad links point to it. The risk is higher if your site already has a suspicious backlink profile or if there’s a large, unnatural pattern.

Best protection:
- Monitor backlinks regularly
- Watch Google Search Console for manual actions/messages
- Disavow clearly spammy links if needed
- Keep your site technically healthy and content-focused

So: possible, but not always effective.

Yes, in some cases they can.

If a competitor points a redirected domain at your site, any penalty or bad signals associated with that domain can follow the redirect and hurt the destination site. In practice, search engines try to detect abuse, but redirects can still cause problems.

More broadly, competitors can also harm you by sending spammy links, filing bad reports, or creating other manipulative signals. The best defense is to monitor backlinks, avoid risky redirects, and use Google Search Console to watch for manual actions or unnatural link warnings. If you suspect negative SEO, document it and file a reconsideration request if needed.

Yes—Google’s +1 can affect SEO, but mostly indirectly.

According to Google, +1s can help friends, contacts, and other users find better results, and Google may also show a +1 count in search results even when it isn’t from your personal network.

However, it’s not something that directly boosts rankings in a simple global “more +1s = higher rank” way. The bigger benefit is likely improved click-through rate and visibility in search results, which can help SEO over time.

So if the button slows your site, it’s not guaranteed to be a major ranking factor. Use it if you want the social/visibility benefit, but don’t expect a direct global ranking boost.

Anti-hotlinking is usually done by checking the HTTP Referer header and blocking image requests that come from other domains.

In Apache/.htaccess, a common approach is:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^http://(.+\.)?yourdomain\.com/ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^$
RewriteRule \.(png|gif|jpg)$ - [F,L]
```

Important:
- Escape the dot in your domain: `yourdomain\.com`
- Make sure the rule matches your file extensions correctly
- Some browsers or tools may send no Referer, so decide whether to allow blank referers

Note: Referer-based blocking is not perfect; it can be spoofed or omitted.

Anti-hotlinking is usually done by checking the HTTP Referer header and serving or redirecting the file only if the request comes from your own domain.

Example in .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^https?://(www\.)?domain\.com/ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^$
RewriteRule \.(jpg|jpeg|gif|png|bmp)$ - [F,L]

This blocks other sites from directly embedding your images. If you want to allow direct browser access too, adjust the conditions carefully.

Important: referer-based blocking is not perfect, because the header can be missing or spoofed. For stronger protection, use signed URLs, tokens, or hotlink protection built into your CDN/server.

Anti-hotlinking is typically done by checking the HTTP Referer header and only allowing requests from your own domain.

For Amazon S3, the recommended approach is to use an S3 bucket policy with the `aws:Referer` condition, rather than serving a replacement HTML file. That way, direct image requests from other sites can be blocked at the bucket level.

Example idea:
- Allow requests only if `Referer` matches your site
- Deny others from fetching the object

Note: Referer-based protection is not perfect, since headers can be missing or spoofed, but it’s the standard simple anti-hotlinking method in S3.

Google bots generally work fine with database-driven sites as long as each important page has a unique, crawlable URL and the content is available in the HTML response.

Key points:
- Use distinct URLs for distinct content, e.g. `/thread?id=101`, not only a single homepage with changing widgets.
- Google can crawl dynamic pages; it does not require “static files,” but the page must be reachable without relying only on JavaScript/Ajax.
- If content is loaded client-side, make sure there’s server-side rendered content or another crawlable fallback.
- Google indexes pages by URL and content, not by “database vs. static.”
- For ads, the page’s HTML/JS loads ad code, and Google uses the page context to choose ads.

So yes: database-driven sites are fine if each page is accessible, indexable, and has meaningful content.

Googlebots crawl database-driven sites the same way they crawl static ones: by following URLs and requesting pages over HTTP.

What matters is that each database-generated page has a unique, crawlable URL. Google doesn’t care if the content comes from MySQL/PHP as long as the server returns normal HTML.

Best practices:
- Use clean, unique URLs for each record/page
- Make sure pages are linked internally or in a sitemap
- Avoid blocking Googlebot in robots.txt if you want indexing
- If you’re logging visits, don’t rely on robots.txt to filter bots; detect bots by user-agent or other checks in your app

So: database-driven is fine. The key is URL structure and accessible HTML, not how the content is stored.

Googlebot can crawl database-driven sites just fine, as long as your pages have crawlable URLs and return normal HTML.

Key points:
- Googlebot follows links; it doesn’t “use” your database directly.
- If your site generates pages from a database, each important page needs a unique, stable URL.
- Avoid hiding content behind forms, login walls, or JavaScript-only rendering unless you also provide crawlable HTML.
- Use robots.txt to allow/disallow sections if needed.
- Make sure pages don’t create endless URL parameters or duplicate content.

If your database pages are reachable by links and accessible without special interaction, Googlebot will index them like any other site.

Search engines can’t reliably read text inside images, so the best way is to provide the same text as real HTML text on the page. If you need the image look, use CSS to overlay the image version on top of the actual text.

That way:
- users see the designed image/text
- bots can read the HTML text
- you avoid “hidden text” penalties

Also add descriptive alt text for important images, but don’t rely on alt/title alone for indexing. If the text is critical for SEO, it should exist in the page markup as normal text.

Yes, there can be an SEO trade-off.

If the content is only loaded by Ajax when the user scrolls, Google may not see it reliably unless it’s also available in the initial HTML or made crawlable another way. That can mean those products/content may not be indexed or fully represented in search results.

So:

- Lazy-load non-essential content: usually fine
- Don’t lazy-load important SEO content if it isn’t otherwise accessible
- Use crawlable techniques if the content matters for search
- Test performance too; lazy loading doesn’t always make the page faster overall

In short: choose carefully what to lazy-load, especially on pages where ranking matters.

No—Google does not prefer HTML sites over WordPress sites, or WordPress over HTML, just because of the platform.

For SEO, Google cares mainly about:
- useful, original content
- fast page load
- mobile friendliness
- clean site structure
- proper titles/meta, headings, internal links
- local SEO signals for a business site
- crawlability and technical health

A hand-coded HTML site can rank just as well as WordPress if it’s well built. WordPress can help because it makes content editing, plugins, and SEO management easier, but it’s not an automatic ranking advantage.

For a small local business, choose the platform that lets you maintain the site easily and keep it fast, secure, and content-rich.

The easiest and SEO-safe way is:

- Change to the new URL structure
- Set up 301 redirects from every old URL to its new equivalent
- Drop the file extensions if possible

That preserves link equity and tells search engines the move is permanent.

Example:
`/picasso/pablo-picasso.html` → `/pablo-picasso/`

Using rewrite rules can keep clean URLs while routing to PHP internally, so visitors won’t see `.php` or `.html`.

Avoid changing URLs without redirects, since that can hurt rankings and break existing links.

The easiest way is usually not to “change PHP URLs” directly, but to use a front controller with URL rewriting.

Typical setup:
1. Create Apache/Nginx rewrite rules so all requests go to `index.php`
2. In `index.php`, define routes like `/products/tables/green/little-wood123/`

For a tiny project, use a microframework such as:
- Slim
- Flight
- Limonade
- Glue

These are lightweight and already support pretty URLs. If you want, you can also write your own simple router, but a microframework is usually faster and cleaner.

`links:www.mysite.com` is not a valid Google search operator. Google treats it like a normal search for the word “links” plus that URL/text.

`link:www.mysite.com` was the old Google operator for showing pages that link to a site, but it’s now very limited and often unreliable.

If you want to check inbound links, better options are:
- Google Search Console → Links report
- SEO tools like Ahrefs, Moz, SEMrush, Majestic

So:
- `link:` = intended backlink operator
- `links:` = just a keyword search
- Best practice = use Search Console or a dedicated backlink tool

Google crawlers can see PHP-generated dynamic content the same way they see any other page: by requesting the URL and reading the HTML your PHP outputs.

Key points:
- PHP runs on the server, so Googlebot does not need to “see” the PHP code.
- It only sees the rendered page content returned by the URL.
- To help Google discover pages, make sure they are linked from other pages or included in a sitemap.
- If a page changes later, Google may notice on its next crawl of that URL. Updating the page content itself is enough; you don’t need a special “dynamic” setup.
- If pages are not linked and not in a sitemap, Google may never find them.

Best practice: use crawlable links for important pages, and use sitemap.xml as a discovery hint, not a guarantee.

Google crawlers can see PHP dynamic content the same way they see any page: they fetch the rendered HTML output from the URL, not the PHP source code.

To help Google crawl dynamic PHP pages:

- Make sure each page has a unique, crawlable URL.
- Return normal HTML when Googlebot requests the page.
- Avoid requiring JavaScript/cookies/login to reveal important content.
- Use an XML sitemap to list your dynamic URLs.
- Ensure pages are linked internally, not only generated by scripts.
- Don’t block Googlebot in robots.txt or by server rules.

If your PHP page changes often, Google may re-crawl it more often, but there’s no guaranteed schedule. Submitting a sitemap usually helps discovery.

For search-generated content, don’t try to index every possible query URL. Google generally avoids indexing internal search result pages.

Better approach:
- Create clean, permanent URLs for important content, e.g. /image/1234 or /tag/blue-tiff
- Link to those pages from your home page, category pages, recent searches, trending searches, or related items
- Use server-side routing or mod_rewrite for known content URLs
- Add internal links so search engines can crawl deeper pages

If you want query pages indexed, only expose a small set of valuable, static-like search/result pages, and make them reachable through normal links. Search engines prefer content pages over endless parameter-based search results.

Create crawlable, permanent URLs for each searchable result set, instead of relying on a hidden dump page or POST-only forms. Use GET parameters or REST-style paths, for example:

- example.com/dogs/coat/brown
- example.com/search.php?coatcolor=brown

Make each common filter/query combination available at its own URL, with unique page titles and content. That way users can bookmark/share results, and search engines can index them.

Avoid redirecting all queries to one generic page; the indexed URL should directly display the results. Also make sure internal links point to these URLs so crawlers can discover them.

For ASP.NET, SEO for database-driven pages means:

1. Give every page unique, DB-filled:
- `<title>`
- `<meta name="description">`
- `<h1>`

2. Use human-readable URLs instead of IDs:
- Bad: `/page.aspx?id=54637`
- Better: `/cats`
- Best: `/products/blue-widget`

3. Store a slug/alias in the database for each record and use that in routing.

4. Make sure pages are crawlable:
- normal HTML content server-side rendered
- no important content only loaded by JavaScript

5. Add sitemap.xml and robots.txt.

6. Avoid duplicate content; each page should have distinct text, title, and description.

In ASP.NET, use routing or rewrite rules to map clean URLs to database records.

Create URLs that reflect a real, unique page for each result set.

If your database-generated pages each contain enough distinct, useful content, it’s fine for search engines to index them. Google generally treats keyword-heavy path URLs and query strings similarly, so switching to query params won’t “hide” the keywords.

Best practice:
- Use short, readable URLs
- Include only a few important terms
- Make sure each URL represents a distinct resource
- Avoid stuffing lots of keywords into the URL
- Don’t rely on URL keywords alone for ranking; use title tags/content too

So, for example, use something like:
`/mazda/miata/1600cc/red/`

rather than a long spammy-looking string.

For SEO on a database-driven ASP.NET site, the main goal is to make pages crawlable and have unique, indexable URLs.

Do this:
- Use “friendly” URLs, not query-string-only URLs if possible.
- Generate unique title tags and meta descriptions per page.
- Make sure important content is in the HTML output, not loaded only by JavaScript.
- Create an XML sitemap and submit it to Google Search Console.
- Use proper heading tags and internal links.
- Avoid duplicate content; use canonical tags where needed.
- Make pages fast and mobile-friendly.

If your site is dynamic, ASP.NET can still do SEO well as long as each record/page has a real URL and meaningful metadata.

In general, yes: .com is often perceived as the most trustworthy/default choice, mostly because it’s the most familiar and widely used. .org is commonly associated with non-profits or organizations, and .net originally meant “network,” but today those meanings are mostly convention.

If you own both .com and .net, it’s usually best to make .com the primary public address and 301-redirect .net to it. That preserves SEO and user access while consolidating branding.

If your business is already established on .net and customers know it, you can keep it live, but .com is typically the better long-term default.

The main practical differences are mostly conventions, not hard rules:

- **.com**: most recognized and usually best for commercial/business sites.
- **.org**: traditionally for organizations, often nonprofits, but widely used by groups/community projects too.
- **.net**: originally for network/Internet service providers, but now often used when the .com is taken.

In practice, people use all three for many purposes. The biggest advantage of **.com** is familiarity: users often default to typing it. If your ideal **.com** is unavailable, a clear, memorable **.net** or **.org** can be better than a poor .com.

So the choice is usually about branding and availability, not strict technical differences.

For .com vs .org vs .net, the main differences are branding, trust, and intended use—not SEO.

- .com: most common, commercial/business use, usually the most recognized and easiest to remember.
- .org: traditionally for organizations/nonprofits, often seen as more “mission” or community oriented.
- .net: originally for network/tech companies, now mostly just an alternative if .com is taken.

SEO-wise, Google generally treats these as generic TLDs, so there’s no built-in ranking boost for any of them. What matters more is content, links, and reputation.

Practical advantage of .com: it’s usually the default people type and may look more authoritative. If you can get the .com, it’s often best for a global brand.

A sudden drop in indexed pages is usually not a technical issue if there are no crawl errors, server/DNS problems, or noindex changes. In your case, the most likely cause is content quality/duplication. If the pages are keyword-replaced or mostly duplicated, Google may deindex them because they don’t add enough unique value.

There isn’t a “workaround” to force indexing. The long-term fix is to improve the pages substantially: add original, useful content, reduce duplication, and make sure each page has a clear purpose and value. Otherwise, the decline may continue.

A sudden drop in pages “indexed” in Google can happen even when the pages are still searchable. It often reflects a quality or crawlability issue rather than a complete deindexing.

Common causes:
- Panda/quality-related demotion
- Weak or duplicate content being devalued
- Crawl issues from broken links or bad redirects
- Poor internal linking to low-value pages

What helped in the resolved case:
- Redirected poor-quality pages to newer, better relevant pages
- Fixed broken links
- Removed links to poor-quality pages from higher-quality pages

Check whether traffic dropped too, and review Search Console for crawl errors, indexing status, and quality signals.

A sudden drop in indexed pages usually means Googlebot is having trouble crawling your site, not that it “decided” to remove pages arbitrarily.

Check:
- DNS/server availability: your note about “Googlebot can’t access your site” and DNS errors is a strong clue.
- robots.txt and meta noindex tags.
- Redirects and broken links.
- Crawl errors in Google Search Console.

A good next step is to spider the site yourself with a tool like Xenu’s Link Sleuth (or Screaming Frog) to find broken links and inaccessible pages. Then fix or redirect them. If DNS/server issues are happening, resolve those first, since Google may stop indexing when it can’t reliably reach your pages.

A sudden drop like that is usually not a technical indexing bug. In the resolved case, the pages were “keyword replaced” and largely duplicate, which Google classifies as low-quality/near-duplicate content.

What to check:
- Search Console: Manual Actions, Security Issues, and Indexing reports
- Crawlability: robots.txt, noindex tags, canonicals, redirects
- Server logs: ensure Googlebot can fetch pages normally
- Content quality: unique value, not just spun/replaced text

If most pages are templated or duplicated, Google may keep reducing them from the index. There isn’t really a workaround other than improving or consolidating the content.

A big drop in reported indexed pages doesn’t always mean pages were actually deindexed. In cases like the resolved thread, it can happen after a quality-related algorithm change such as Panda, or when Google recalculates which URLs it considers worth showing in index reports.

Common causes:
- Low-quality or duplicate pages being dropped from reporting
- Crawlability/indexation issues
- Broken links or poor internal linking
- Pages being redirected, noindexed, or removed

What to check:
- Google Search Console coverage/indexing reports
- robots.txt, meta noindex, canonical tags
- 404/redirect issues
- Thin/duplicate content

Improving site quality and internal linking often helps over time.

If Google can find the pages in a site search, the index is probably fine and the drop to 0 in Webmaster Tools/Search Console is often a reporting glitch or sitemap issue.

Check:
- Sitemap status/errors in the Issues column
- Whether the sitemap loads in a browser
- Use the Test Sitemap feature
- Confirm the sitemap URLs exactly match the live/indexed pages
- Look at Health > Index Status

If everything looks valid, it may just be a temporary Search Console blip and can correct itself within 24 hours.

You still use a meta description because Google does not always show page text.

- when the search terms are not clearly on the page

- when it wants a clearer, more accurate snippet for users

Meta descriptions are still useful because they influence the snippet Google shows and can improve click-through rate.

If the PDFs are truly removed and won’t come back, a 410 Gone is usually better than a 404 because it tells Google the URL was intentionally retired.

You can still show a helpful HTML page for users on that URL, such as:
- a short explanation that the file is no longer available
- links to similar products/documents
- a search or category page

Noindex/nofollow is not needed just because it’s a PDF. Google can index PDFs. The key is whether the file should remain accessible:
- keep it: return 200
- permanently removed: return 410
- temporarily unavailable: return 404 or 503

If the partner’s page and site are truly gone and now return 404, you usually don’t need to do anything.

Search engines won’t keep following a dead page, and the backlink will typically drop out of your backlink profile over time. No disavow is needed just because the source page disappeared.

Only consider action if:
- the old URL redirects somewhere questionable,
- the site reappears with spammy content,
- or you still have a live link from another page on that domain.

Otherwise, just leave it.

Use a 301 redirect in the server config/.htaccess for each deleted URL, pointing to the new page or file.

For example:

Redirect 301 /fa/home.html /fa/
Redirect 301 /en/home.html /fa/

If you want to redirect multiple old pages, add one line per URL. For WordPress “pretty” URLs, make sure permalinks are enabled first.

Note: if your site is actually on Nginx, .htaccess will not work there; you must add the redirect in the Nginx config instead.

For deleted content, don’t use a 301 unless there’s a clear replacement page with equivalent content.

Best practice:
- If the content is truly gone and not replaced: return 410 Gone.
- If the content has a real replacement: use 301 redirect to that new page.
- If you can, keep a helpful custom “gone” page that explains the removal and offers links to:
  - Home page
  - Sitemap
  - Search
  - Similar content

SEO-wise, 410 tells search engines the page has been intentionally removed. A 404 is also acceptable, but 410 is stronger for permanent deletion.

A 301 redirect is generally not a good choice if the replacement page is unrelated.

If the deleted pages are not similar to the homepage, redirecting them there can create a poor user experience and may not preserve much SEO value anyway. In those cases, a 410 Gone is often the safer option because it clearly tells search engines the content has been removed permanently.

Best practice:
- Redirect only to a closely related page if one exists.
- If no relevant replacement exists, use 410 Gone or a normal 404.
- Avoid sending all deleted pages to the homepage just to “keep link juice.”

To keep Google and most other search engines from indexing a site under construction:

1. Use `robots.txt` at the site root:
   - Block the whole site:
     ```txt
     User-agent: *
     Disallow: /
     ```
   - Or block only specific folders/pages:
     ```txt
     User-agent: *
     Disallow: /admin/
     Disallow: /private_file.html
     ```

2. Add a `noindex` meta tag or HTTP header on the under-construction page:
   ```html
   <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
   ```

3. If the pages are already indexed, use Google Search Console to request removal.

Important: `robots.txt` asks crawlers not to crawl; it does not secure the content. For sensitive pages, protect them with authentication or restrict access at the server level.

To keep a site under construction out of search engines, use a `noindex` directive on every page that should not be indexed.

Best options:
- Add this to the page HTML:
  `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">`
- Or send an HTTP header:
  `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`

If you want only the homepage indexed, leave the homepage with:
`<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">`

And put `noindex, nofollow` on all other pages.

Note: `Disallow: /` in `robots.txt` blocks crawling, but it does not guarantee pages won’t appear in search results if they’re discovered elsewhere.

- Optionally add schema.org structured data where appropriate

So your repeated widget text on every post is usually fine.

Use mod_rewrite in your `.htaccess`:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^script/(\w+)\.png$ /script/image.php?name=$1 [L]
```

This rewrites:

`/script/esqew.png` → `/script/image.php?name=esqew`

Notes:
- `(\w+)` matches letters, numbers, and underscore.
- `[L]` means “last rule.”
- If your `.htaccess` is inside `/script/`, then use:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^(\w+)\.png$ image.php?name=$1 [L]
```

Use an external redirect for the old URLs, then keep your new rewrite rules.

Example:

RewriteEngine On

# Old links -> new /1/ URLs
RewriteRule ^([^/]+)\.htm$ /1/$1.htm [R=301,L]
RewriteRule ^([^/]+)\.htm/([0-9.]+)$ /1/$1.htm/$2 [R=301,L]

# New internal rewrites
RewriteRule ^1/([^/]+)\.htm$ index.php?c=$1 [NC,L]
RewriteRule ^1/([^/]+)\.htm/([0-9.]+)$ index.php?c=$1&amt=$2 [NC,L]
RewriteRule ^2/([^/]+)\.htm$ index2.php?c=$1 [NC,L]
RewriteRule ^2/([^/]+)\.htm/([0-9.]+)$ index2.php?c=$1&amt=$2 [NC,L]

Use 301 if the move is permanent. Put the old-link redirects above the new rewrite rules.

In general, nofollow is not a good idea for your own internal tag/label links.

- Use noindex on tag/label archive pages only if you don’t want them in Google.
- Do not use nofollow on internal links to your own pages; it blocks PageRank flow and doesn’t help SEO.
- If the tag/label pages are thin, duplicate, or low-value, noindex them.
- If they’re useful landing pages with unique content, keep them indexable.

For a big tag cloud:
- Prefer reducing the size or removing it from global sidebar/footer.
- Keep the links if they help users and crawlers.
- Noindex the tag cloud page itself if it’s just a list of links.

So: noindex can make sense; nofollow usually does not.

For a one-time-use, high-traffic site, AdSense is usually not the best fit.

Why:
- AdSense tends to perform poorly unless you have ongoing traffic and strong pageview volume.
- It’s especially weak if the site’s audience isn’t a great match for Google’s ad inventory.
- The thread you shared notes even very high-traffic sites can be disappointed by AdSense.

Better options for a temporary spike:
- Direct sponsorships or sold placements
- Affiliate links if the traffic is intent-driven
- A simple CPA/lead-gen offer
- If traffic is huge and short-lived, a premium ad network or direct-buy campaign may beat AdSense

If the site is truly one-time-use, consider whether the goal is monetization or just covering costs; direct deals usually win.

Changing your domain can affect rankings, but not because of “PageRank” in the old toolbar sense. The main risk is losing signals during the move.

If you do a proper domain migration:
- 301 redirect every old URL to the matching new URL
- keep content and page structure as consistent as possible
- update internal links, canonicals, sitemap, and Search Console
- avoid large unrelated changes at the same time

Then most value can transfer, though temporary ranking drops are common.

So: yes, a domain change can affect your search visibility, but a well-executed move should minimize the impact.

A domain change can affect SEO temporarily, but it usually does not permanently hurt PageRank by itself.

From the thread: Google may look at registration history, WHOIS, and nameserver changes as trust signals, so a registrar or ownership change can be a factor. But in practice, changing registrars/registrant info has very little long-term impact on rankings.

What matters most:
- keeping the same content and URL structure
- using proper 301 redirects if URLs change
- not losing backlinks
- avoiding spammy hosting/nameserver patterns

So: registrar change alone is generally safe for SEO, but expect possible short-term fluctuation.

Changing servers/IP addresses alone usually has little to no direct SEO impact, as long as the site remains available and the URLs/content stay the same.

What matters most:
- Keep the same domain and URL structure
- Avoid downtime during the move
- Preserve page speed and stability
- Make sure DNS changes are correct
- Don’t accidentally change robots.txt, redirects, or canonical tags

Search engines may briefly re-crawl the site after the IP change, but rankings typically stay stable if the site is accessible and unchanged.

If you are actually changing the domain name, that’s a different case and can affect SEO much more.

Changing to a keyword-rich domain is usually not worth it for SEO.

A few points:
- A 301 redirect from the old domain to the new one will usually pass most, but not all, link equity.
- Exact-match/keyword domains don’t provide a big ranking boost anymore, and they can look spammy.
- A short, brandable domain like `companyname.com` is often better for users and long-term SEO.

If you want to target a keyword, the better approach is:
- keep `companyname.com`
- optimize page titles, headings, content, internal links, and metadata
- create a relevant section like `companyname.com/main-keyword/` if it makes sense for site structure

So: keep the current domain and focus on on-page SEO and content quality.

Use 301 redirects from the old domain to the new one. That preserves any existing SEO value/backlinks and tells search engines the move is permanent.

Don’t start from scratch unless you have a strong reason to abandon the old domain. If both domains serve the same content without redirects, you risk duplicate-content/confusion issues.

Also:
- Set the preferred canonical URL on the new site
- Update internal links, sitemap, and Search Console
- Keep the old domain active for a while to catch old links/bookmarks

If you later decide the old domain isn’t needed, you can drop it after the move has been indexed and stabilized.

If you’re changing a domain name, the practical steps are usually:

1. Register the new domain.
2. Lower DNS TTL on the old domain if possible.
3. Update DNS records to point the new domain to your hosting/server.
4. Install/configure SSL for the new domain.
5. Update your website/app settings, links, and hardcoded URLs.
6. Set up 301 redirects from old URLs to new ones.
7. Update email records/services if the domain is used for email.
8. Verify analytics, Search Console, and third-party integrations.
9. Test everything end to end.

If you want, I can give you a checklist for WordPress specifically.

Practical steps:

1. Buy/register the new domain.
2. Point the new domain to the same hosting/site content as the old domain.
3. Update the site config/CMS so it recognizes the new domain as the primary one.
4. Set up 301 redirects from every old URL to the matching new URL.
5. Update internal links, canonical tags, sitemap, and any hardcoded references to the old domain.
6. Notify Google Search Console/Bing Webmaster Tools and resubmit the sitemap.
7. Keep the old domain active long enough for redirects and bookmarks to work.

In short: new domain points to the same site, old domain redirects permanently to the new one.

Your main domain may still appear as an addon domain because, in many shared hosting setups, the “main” domain is just the first/primary addon domain attached to the account. The control panel doesn’t always distinguish them the way you expect.

If your goal is to keep it out of search results, use a noindex tag on the main domain’s pages, for example:

That tells search engines not to index that domain’s page, while leaving your other addon domains unaffected.
