You can’t “direct HTTPS requests to HTTP” while still using the expired cert. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS/SSL, so if the certificate is expired, the TLS handshake will fail before any HTTP request is sent.

Options:
- Renew/replace the certificate.
- Temporarily use plain HTTP on a separate endpoint/port.
- If this is only for testing, disable certificate verification in the client. This is unsafe for production.

You also can’t run SSL “on HTTP” — the result is simply HTTPS.

If the HTTPS cert is expired, browsers will warn before any redirect is honored, so you can’t reliably “direct HTTPS to HTTP” from the same endpoint.

What you can do:
- Renew/replace the cert, then issue a 301 redirect from HTTPS to HTTP if you really need that.
- If the domain is being retired, simply let the cert expire and remove DNS records (A/AAAA/CNAME/MX) so users won’t hit the old site.
- If you want to prevent misuse of old private keys, revoke the cert before it expires.

Bottom line: expired SSL certs cannot cleanly redirect HTTPS to HTTP; fix the cert or retire the domain.

You can’t avoid the cert warning when someone connects to `https://www.domain.com` with an invalid/mismatched certificate.

Reason: HTTPS redirection only happens after the TLS handshake. The browser must first verify the certificate, and if it doesn’t match `www.domain.com`, it warns before any HTTP redirect can be sent.

Your options:
- Get a certificate valid for both `domain.com` and `www.domain.com` using SAN/subjectAltName.
- Or get a wildcard cert like `*.domain.com`.
- Then redirect `www` to non-`www` in Nginx.

If you only have a cert for `domain.com`, `https://www.domain.com` will always warn first.

If you mean changing a nameserver host from a static IP to a domain name: DNS normally uses the nameserver’s hostname, not just its IP.

You register the nameserver hostname with its “glue” IP at the registrar. The registry stores both the hostname and IP. If the nameserver’s IP changes later, you must update the glue record at your registrar; otherwise resolvers may not be able to find that nameserver.

So the process is:

1. Register nameserver name: ns1.example.com  
2. Provide its IP address to the registrar  
3. If the IP changes, update it at the registrar

This is how DNS can still locate the nameserver after its IP changes.

In the resolved thread, Firefox/Firebug showed an “uncaught exception” plus other page errors. A script error can stop later scripts from running, including Google Custom Search.

Things to check:
- Fix any JavaScript errors in your homepage first.
- Wrap jQuery code in `$(document).ready(...)`.
- Verify CSS/JS files are loading with the correct MIME types.
- Make sure your page’s search result container and scripts are included correctly.

If you mean normal Google indexing, also verify:
- Your site is public and crawlable
- No `robots.txt` or `noindex` blocking
- You’ve submitted the site to Search Console

Most likely, Google just hasn’t indexed your site yet. Even if your keywords are present, it can take time for Google to discover, crawl, and rank a new website.

To improve visibility:
- Make sure your site is publicly accessible and not blocked by robots.txt or noindex tags.
- Submit your site to Google Search Console.
- Get other sites to link to yours.
- Consider adding your site to reputable web directories.

Also, searching by domain name doesn’t guarantee immediate results if Google hasn’t indexed it yet. Patience is part of it, but making sure the site is crawlable helps too.

This usually happens after moving from Blogspot to a custom domain when Google hasn’t fully reindexed the site yet, or the migration wasn’t set up correctly.

Check these first:
- In Google Search Console, verify the new domain and submit the XML sitemap.
- Make sure the old Blogspot URL 301-redirects to the new .com pages.
- Confirm your pages are not blocked by robots.txt or meta noindex.
- Use “Inspect URL” in Search Console and request indexing for key pages.
- Keep the old Blogspot site active long enough for Google to pass signals.

Also, rankings often drop temporarily after a domain move. It can take weeks or months to recover.

If your blog is already indexed in normal Google Search, the main issue is likely just Google Blog Search/Blog indexing delay or limited coverage. You’ve already done the right things: pinging, verifying in Webmaster Tools, and submitting manually.

What to check:

If Google won’t fetch or index the redesigned homepage, first check for anything blocking it:

- robots.txt: make sure the page isn’t disallowed
- meta robots: ensure there’s no `noindex`
- Canonical tag: confirm it points to the correct homepage URL
- Redirects: verify the homepage returns a normal 200 OK, not a bad redirect loop
- JavaScript: if the new design relies heavily on JS, Google may have trouble rendering it

Also submit a sitemap.xml in Search Console and use “Fetch as Google” / “URL Inspection” again after fixing.

“Not selected” in Google Search Console usually means URLs are either:

- redirects to other pages, or
- very similar/duplicate pages Google chose not to index.

So if you fixed duplicates with 301 redirects, that won’t necessarily lower the “not selected” count. Those URLs are still in the report because they now redirect, which is expected.

This is generally not a problem. It usually means Google is recognizing your canonical URLs correctly.

What to check:
- Make sure your important pages return 200 OK
- Make sure internal links point to the canonical URLs
- Keep the sitemap listing only the final canonical pages

If you want, I can help you review specific examples from your report.

Search engines mainly care about the content and links they can access, not whether your CSS is loaded by JavaScript.

So loading an enhanced stylesheet with JS should not cause major indexing or ranking problems by itself.

Possible issues only arise if:
- important content is hidden or removed when JS fails
- CSS/JS is used to cloak content or mislead crawlers
- the page becomes hard to render or access because of JS dependencies

For normal progressive enhancement, this is fine. Keep core content in plain HTML, make sure it’s visible without JS, and you should be okay.

If pages are “not searchable by Google,” usually one of these is blocking indexing:

- `noindex` meta tag or HTTP header
- `robots.txt` disallow
- canonical pointing elsewhere
- content loaded only via scripts or iframes
- page requires login / has crawl errors

If you want only part of a page hidden, note Google can still index text it can see in HTML/JS. The most reliable options are:
- keep private data out of the page HTML entirely
- load it after login
- use separate pages/subpages for public text vs. private author info
- if using iframes, block the iframe URL with `noindex`

If your pages show up in `site:yourdomain.com` searches but not in normal queries, Google is likely indexing them but not ranking them well.

Common causes:
- Duplicate or near-duplicate title tags, meta descriptions, or page content
- Weak/irrelevant content for the search query
- Low authority/backlinks compared with competing pages
- Technical issues: noindex tags, canonical tags, robots.txt blocks

What to do:
1. Check Google Search Console for indexing/crawl issues.
2. Make titles and descriptions unique per page.
3. Search a very unique sentence from the page in quotes; if it doesn’t appear, it may be treated as duplicate/supplemental.
4. Improve content quality and internal linking.
5. Submit updated pages in Search Console.

If you want, I can help you diagnose a specific URL.

Yes — robots.txt alone does not remove already-indexed URLs. It only tells crawlers not to crawl the page, but Google can still keep and show the URL in results if it was discovered before.

Best practice:
1. If you want a page removed from search, allow Google to crawl it.
2. Add a noindex meta tag or, better, an HTTP X-Robots-Tag: noindex.
3. Once Google has recrawled and dropped it, you can optionally block it in robots.txt if you still want to prevent crawling.

If the page is urgent, you can also use Google Search Console’s Removals tool for temporary hiding, but that is not a permanent fix.

So: remove the Disallow for pages you want deindexed, add noindex, then request removal only if needed for speed.

Google’s old WMT/Search Console “Site Performance” data can stop updating for long periods, and in some cases the feature was phased out entirely. So if you’re seeing no updates for weeks, it’s likely not a problem with your crawl rate or traffic.

- Check the newer Search Console reports for performance/crawl info

In short: the lack of updates is usually on Google’s side, and that old report isn’t reliable anymore.

A few things to check:

- If the redesign is JavaScript-heavy, Google may struggle to render it. Test with “View Source” and Google’s URL Inspection tool.

Also verify the homepage returns a proper 200 OK and canonical points to itself.

To get Google to recognize your domain instead of the IP, set up a 301 redirect from the IP address to your domain.

This tells Google that the domain is the permanent version and transfers indexing signals to it.

Example for Apache (.htaccess in your site root):

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^121\.12\.12\.123
RewriteRule (.*) http://www.mydomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]

Also:
- Make sure your domain points to the same site
- Add the domain to Google Search Console
- Submit a sitemap for the domain
- Let Google recrawl the site; it can take time

If you mean “How do I make Google know my domain exists?”:

1. Set up Google Search Console for your domain.  
2. Verify ownership.  
3. Submit your sitemap.xml.  
4. Make sure your site is crawlable:
   - no accidental noindex
   - no blocked robots.txt
   - working internal links
5. Get a few legit backlinks or social mentions.
6. Add quality content and wait—Google will find it.

To make Google “know” your domain/subdomain, add DNS records for it.

For a Google service like Gmail, set up a **CNAME** record for the subdomain you want, pointing to:

`ghs.google.com`

Example:
- Host/Name: `mail`
- Type: `CNAME`
- Value/Target: `ghs.google.com`

Then enable/use that URL in your Google Apps / Workspace control panel.

This works for Google services like mail, sites, docs, etc.

There’s no fixed time, but after submitting a sitemap, Google often takes a couple of weeks to start indexing URLs. Without a sitemap, it can take 30+ days or longer. If your sitemap has no errors, “0 indexed” after 4 days is still normal.

A few things affect speed:
- site age and authority
- crawlability/robots.txt
- internal linking
- content quality and uniqueness

You can help by:
- making sure pages are reachable by links
- using Google Search Console to inspect URLs
- requesting indexing for important pages

So, expect weeks rather than days in many cases.

There’s no fixed timeframe. Google may index some URLs in days or weeks, but it can also take months, and submitting a sitemap does not guarantee indexing.

In the resolved thread, the main issue wasn’t timing: the sitemap contained URLs that 301-redirected to different pages. Google indexed the final destination URLs, not the redirected ones, so Webmaster Tools showed few of the submitted URLs as indexed.

Check that your sitemap contains only live, canonical URLs that return 200 OK, not redirects or blocked pages. Also make sure your robots.txt is valid. If the URLs are correct, indexing still depends on quality, crawlability, and site authority.

Submitting a sitemap does not guarantee instant indexing. Google may discover your URLs quickly, but actual indexing can take from a few hours to several days, and sometimes longer, depending on site quality, crawl frequency, and whether the pages are new or changed.

A sitemap mainly helps Google find your content more easily; it doesn’t force indexing. If you want faster results, make sure:

- the sitemap is valid and submitted in Search Console
- pages are crawlable and not blocked by robots.txt/noindex
- internal links point to the pages
- content is unique and useful

You can monitor progress in Google Search Console under Pages/Indexing.

If Google is indexing the site but not showing it for your brand name, the likely issue is relevance and site structure, not crawling.

Key fixes:
- Improve title tags and on-page text so your site clearly says what it is.
- Add an About page with substantial content.
- Make sure every page links back to the homepage.
- Add and submit an XML sitemap in Google Search Console.
- Clean up your URLs: avoid .php, query strings, spaces, and special characters. Use simple, readable URLs.

Example:
`/political-science/`  
instead of  
`/tableDriver.php?table=polscience&name=Political%20Science`

Also ensure your homepage has clear text in an H1, not only in a paragraph tag.

Google often ignores the meta description/title if it thinks another snippet is more relevant, especially when pages have very similar titles/descriptions.

Things to check:
- Make each page title unique.
- Make each meta description unique and clearly match the page content.
- Ensure the page content is crawlable and not blocked by JS, overlays, or unusual markup.
- Use Search Console to request indexing, but 3 days may be too short for Google to fully recrawl and update.

Also, Google may have cached the old version. Check the cached copy/date in search results or Search Console crawl stats.

Avoid trying to hide text from Google; that can look like cloaking.

Google may be ignoring your title/meta description and generating its own snippet from page content. That’s normal.

What to check:
- Each page has a unique, accurate `<title>` and `<meta name="description">`
- Your page is indexable: no `noindex`, `nofollow`, blocked by robots.txt, or canonical pointing elsewhere
- The content is visible to Googlebot (not hidden behind JS, login, or loaded only after scripts)
- Titles/descriptions aren’t duplicated, too long, or unrelated to the page

Even if everything is correct, Google can still choose different text for search results. You can’t force it.

Google Search Console’s “Change of address” is picky about verification.

What usually causes this:
- `example.com` and `www.example.com` are treated as separate properties.
- They must be verified with the same method.
- The “new” domain (`example2.com`) must also be verified in the same account.

What to do:
1. Add both `http://example.com` and `http://www.example.com` as separate properties.
2. Verify them using the same method (for example, DNS TXT for both).
3. Make sure `example2.com` is also verified.
4. Retry the change of address from the exact property for the old domain.

If you verified one with HTML file and the other with DNS, reverify so both match.

Google treats .se as a country-code TLD for Sweden, so you can’t change its geo-targeting to the Netherlands in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console.

Your options are:

- Use a .nl domain for the Dutch market
- Or use a generic TLD Google allows geo-targeting on, then set the target to the Netherlands

Google will not override the .se country association based on backlinks or content signals. So no, it won’t “eventually” switch to the Netherlands on its own.

Yes, search engines can index different subdomains on different hosting servers, as long as they can crawl them and they aren’t blocked by robots.txt or meta noindex.

But in your case, if a subdomain contains only translated titles while the body/UGC stays in the original language, Google may treat that as mixed-language/low-quality and index it poorly or not at all. Search engines do not automatically “understand” that one subdomain should be crawled only for one language version unless you explicitly separate the fully translated pages.

Best practice:
- Put fully translated content on separate language URLs/subdomains.
- Use hreflang between language versions.
- Use noindex for pages that are only partially translated.
- Don’t rely on a different host/server to change indexing behavior; hosting location doesn’t matter much.

If you removed the blocking robots metatags, Google may still need time to recrawl and reindex the site. Also, “not showing up” doesn’t always mean “not indexed.”

Check these first:

A few notes:

- Crawled ≠ indexed immediately.

If Google already knows about the pages, removing the block in robots.txt alone may not remove them from search results. In fact, Google needs to be able to crawl a page to see a noindex tag.

Best practice:
- If you want pages removed from Google: allow crawling, then add a noindex meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header.
- Keep the pages accessible to Google until they are recrawled and dropped from the index.
- After that, you can block them in robots.txt if you still want to prevent crawling.

Use Google’s Removals tool only for temporary hiding or urgent removal. It is not the main long-term fix.

If searching for `www.caterboxgroup.co.uk` returns results, your site is already indexed.

The keywords shown in Webmaster Tools/Search Console can come from pages linking to your site, not just from text on your own pages. So terms like “domain” and “registered” may reflect anchor text or context from inbound links.

Since the site is relatively new, it may take time for Google to rank it for the terms you want. Keep adding good content, get relevant backlinks, and make sure your pages are crawlable.

- Add canonical tags on pages that are accessible in both HTTP and HTTPS to avoid duplicate-content SEO issues.

So: one tracking setup is enough; no duplicate profile is required.

In cPanel File Manager there’s no built-in “grep” or code search across many files.

Search engines usually discover new subdomains automatically, often fairly quickly. The easiest way to help is to link to each subdomain from a page on the main domain that Google crawls often. That gives Google a path to find the new site.

You generally do not need to create a separate sitemap for every subdomain just to get it indexed. Also, changing the subdomain itself won’t make it get discovered faster.

If you want faster indexing:
- make sure the subdomain is publicly accessible
- link to it from the parent domain
- submit a sitemap if appropriate
- optionally use Google Search Console after verification

Services that create subsites/subdomains usually get them indexed the same way any site does: by making the pages crawlable.

- Make the subdomain publicly accessible with a normal 200 OK response
- Link to it from other indexed pages
- Submit its sitemap in Google Search Console / Bing Webmaster Tools
- Ensure robots.txt and meta tags don’t block crawling
- Use a rel=canonical tag if there are duplicate versions

Search engines don’t need special handling just because a site is a subdomain. If the subdomain is publicly reachable and linked, Google/Bing will usually crawl and index it like any other site.

To help it get indexed:
- Make sure DNS and web server are set up correctly.
- Ensure the subdomain returns normal HTML pages, not redirects or errors.
- Don’t block it in robots.txt or via noindex tags.
- Add links to it from other indexed pages.

If those classifieds are meant to be indexed, let Google crawl them normally and keep the URLs stable. When an ad expires, don’t just let it 404 immediately if there may be value in the page/history.

Google may not be “reading” your meta title/description because they are only hints, not guarantees. A few key points:

- Google primarily uses the visible page content and the HTML `<title>` tag.
- `<meta name="description">` is often used only as a search snippet suggestion.
- `<meta name="title">` is generally ignored by Google; it’s redundant with `<title>`.
- If your page content is thin, duplicated, blocked, or rendered oddly (JS, robots.txt, noindex), Google may not index it well.

Check:
1. Page has a real `<title>` tag.
2. Description is in `<meta name="description" content="...">`.
3. Page is crawlable and indexable.
4. Content is unique and visible in HTML.

A new domain often takes time to earn trust and get fully crawled, especially after moving from Blogspot to a custom domain. Common causes of poor indexing:

- noindex/meta robots or robots.txt blocking pages
- incorrect 301 redirects from the old Blogspot URLs
- missing or weak internal links
- thin/duplicate content
- not enough external links/citations yet
- sitemap not submitted or crawl errors in Search Console

What to check:
1. In Google Search Console, inspect a few URLs and see if Google can index them.
2. Submit an XML sitemap.
3. Verify old .blogspot URLs 301 redirect to the matching .com pages.
4. Make sure pages are crawlable and not set to noindex.
5. Build quality links and wait a bit; new sites can be slow to rank.

A new blog with only ~40 posts can be under-indexed simply because Google hasn’t decided it’s high-quality enough yet. The main things to check are:

- Posting consistency: regular growth helps a new site.
- Content depth: thin posts can be ignored.
- Uniqueness: avoid duplicate or near-duplicate content.
- Technical issues: crawl errors, robots.txt, noindex tags, canonical tags, soft 404s.

The drop after an update usually means Google re-evaluated quality, not just the sitemap. Make sure the site has strong original content, good internal linking, and no indexing blockers in Search Console. If the number of indexed pages keeps falling, inspect the pages Google is excluding and why.

Yes—if you want Google to stop indexing specific pages, robots.txt alone is not the best tool.

Why:
- Disallow in robots.txt blocks crawling, not necessarily indexing.
- Google can still show the URL in search if it knows the page exists from links or past crawling.

Best practice:
1. Remove the Disallow rule for those pages.
2. Add a meta robots tag on the page:
   - `noindex` to prevent indexing
   - `nofollow` only if you also want Google not to follow links on that page
3. Make sure Google can crawl the page to see the `noindex`.

If you need it removed quickly, you can use Google Search Console’s removal tool, but that is usually temporary unless the page is also noindexed or returns 404/410.

Use a new domain when:
- the brand or project is fully separate

The motive of sending spam text is usually to send unwanted messages to many people, often to advertise, scam, or annoy recipients. In contrast, targeted, relevant messages sent with permission are generally not considered spam. If the text is unsolicited, irrelevant, or sent in bulk, it’s more likely to be viewed as spam.

Best option: use responsive design on the same domain/URL if possible.

If you do need a separate mobile site, a subdomain like m.example.com is generally better than registering a new .mobi domain. It’s more familiar to users, feels more trustworthy, and keeps your brand consistent.

Common motives for sending spam texts include:

- Malware delivery: getting you to click malicious links or install apps
- Fraud/scams: fake prizes, delivery notices, or urgent account warnings
- Identity theft: collecting personal information
- Advertising: promoting products or services cheaply and at scale

You can’t force Google to index images. A sitemap only tells Google what exists; it doesn’t guarantee indexing.

To improve image indexing:
- Make sure images are linked from crawlable HTML pages, not only in XML sitemaps.
- Use strong internal linking so Google can discover them easily.
- Earn inbound links to build site reputation.
- Ensure images are unique, useful, and not blocked by robots.txt or noindex.
- Provide good page context: captions, alt text, surrounding text.

If the site is new, slow indexing is normal. For large sites, Google may index only part of it at first and expand over time as the site gains trust and links.

Google isn’t “pulling keywords from only two pages” so much as it’s choosing a few pages it thinks best represent your site.

For a news aggregator, this often happens because most pages are highly dynamic and short-lived. Google may see the site as changing frequently, so only the most stable or prominent pages get strong importance signals.

What to do:
- Make sure each important page has unique, crawlable content.
- Use a clear internal linking structure to show which pages matter most.
- Keep important pages available longer, if possible.
- Submit a clean XML sitemap and ensure it’s accurate.
- Check Google Search Console for crawl/indexing issues.

Also, `site:` results show importance, not necessarily search relevance.

To improve image indexing, focus on making images easier for search engines to understand and faster to crawl:

- Use descriptive file names: `red-running-shoes.jpg` instead of `IMG_1234.jpg`
- Add clear alt text that describes the image
- Keep image files small by compressing them without losing quality
- Use the right format: JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics/transparency
- Make sure images are accessible in HTML, not hidden behind scripts
- Include images in an image sitemap if possible
- Use responsive images so page speed stays fast

Since you’re on a hosted CMS, you may not control caching headers, so optimizing file size and metadata is your best option.

This is normal. Google doesn’t treat multiple words as “must all match” unless you force it to.

If you want both words required, use:
- quotes for an exact phrase: `"another keyword" site:mysite.com`
- or explicit operators, depending on intent

So more results with two keywords does not mean Google is “pulling from only two pages”; it’s just using broader matching and relevance ranking.

Best practice is to assume the site is still compromised and clean it in this order:

1. Take the site offline or restrict access.
2. Restore from a known-clean backup if you have one.
3. Compare current files and database against a pre-hack copy to find all changes.
4. Check for backdoors, not just visible malware.
5. Update the CMS, plugins/extensions, themes, and server software.
6. Change all passwords: hosting, FTP/SFTP, admin, database, SSH.
7. Review permissions and disable unnecessary write access.
8. Scan the site with a malware scanner or your host’s security tools.
9. Find and fix the entry point to prevent reinfection.

Scanning on upload is not enough; you need to stop the attack path and harden access. Lock down admin areas, use SFTP/SSH instead of plain FTP, and restrict FTP by IP if possible.

Removing the malicious code is only a temporary fix if you don’t close the entry point.

- Joomla logs
- Database logs if available
Look for suspicious uploads, admin logins, or requests to vulnerable pages.

2. Patch and update

3. Change credentials

- If you can’t change FTP password, ask your host immediately.

4. Rebuild cleanly
- Replace core Joomla files with a fresh official copy.
- Reinstall trusted extensions from known sources.
- Restore only clean content, not infected files.

5. Harden
- Restrict file permissions.
- Disable file editing in Joomla admin.
- Use WAF/security plugin, but don’t rely on it alone.

If you want `domain.com` (the root/apex) to follow a changing IP, the DNS provider must update the A record dynamically. A CNAME cannot be used at the root in standard DNS.

Typical setup:
- `domain.com` -> dynamic A record updated by your DDNS provider
- `www.domain.com` -> CNAME to `domain.com`

If your registrar only offers forwarding, it can redirect `www` to another URL, but it won’t solve dynamic IP DNS for the root domain.

So the options are:
1. Use a DDNS provider that updates the apex A record, or
2. Get a static IP, or
3. Use `www` as the main hostname and redirect the root to `www` if your registrar supports it.

Google Search Console’s “Change of Address” only works for root-level domains, not subdomains. So you can’t use it to move `aaaa.domain.com` to `newdomain.com`.

What you should do instead:
- Set up a 301 redirect from `aaaa.domain.com` to `www.newdomain.com`
- Also redirect `newdomain.com` to `www.newdomain.com`

If you can’t edit `.htaccess`, contact your hosting provider or use their domain mapping/control panel—many platforms can create the redirect for you automatically.  
If all you can add is HTML, that’s not ideal; a server-side 301 redirect is the correct solution for SEO and traffic transfer.

Also, linking out with dofollow does not normally penalize your page. Google’s concern is mainly with spammy or manipulative link practices, not the presence of outgoing dofollow links.

The most common basic Apache .htaccess redirects are:

- Redirect 301 /old-page.html /new-page.html  
  Permanent redirect for one page.

- Redirect 302 /old-page.html /new-page.html  
  Temporary redirect.

- RedirectMatch 301 ^/old-section/(.*)$ /new-section/$1  
  Pattern-based redirect using regex.

- RewriteEngine On  
  RewriteRule ^old-page/?$ /new-page/ [R=301,L]  
  More flexible and widely used.

For SEO, the key is the HTTP 301/302 response, not whether it’s done in .htaccess or PHP. Search engines care about the redirect status code and destination, not the implementation. .htaccess is often preferred for simple server-side redirects because it happens before PHP runs.

There isn’t a single “standard” set of Apache `.htaccess` redirects, because redirect rules depend on your site structure and goals. The most basic and commonly used ones are:

- Redirect one page to another:
```apache
Redirect 301 /old-page.html /new-page.html
```

- Redirect an entire site/domain:
```apache
Redirect 301 / https://www.example.com/
```

- Rewrite with mod_rewrite:
```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^old-page/?$ /new-page [R=301,L]
```

- Force HTTPS:
```apache
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} off
RewriteRule ^ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

- Force www or non-www:
```apache
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^ https://www.example.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

Use 301 for permanent redirects. There’s no universal list, just common patterns.

The rule itself is fine, but in `httpd.conf` the pattern is matched against the filesystem path, not the URL, so `^/site/(.*)` won’t behave as you expect.

If you’re doing per-directory rewriting, put it in `.htaccess` instead:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^site/(.*) /~username/site/$1 [PT]
```

Also make sure `mod_rewrite` is enabled and that `AllowOverride` permits rewrites for that directory.

If you want to redirect all matching paths to the homepage, your pattern should capture “any number of characters,” not just one.

In mod_rewrite, `(.)` matches exactly one character. Use `(.*)` instead.

Example:
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^a3ff/(.*) https://yourdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]

If you want everything under those paths to go to the homepage, use:
RewriteRule ^a3ff/.*$ https://yourdomain.com/ [R=301,L]

Also make sure the target URL is a full URL including `http://` or `https://`.

This matches both `/a` and `/a/`, `/a/a` and `/a/a/`, etc., so you only need one rule per path depth.

Yes — for a dynamic URL, match the path and the query string separately. Your best solution is:

RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} ^q=customer%20reference&f= [NC]
RewriteRule ^dyn/$ /customer-references/? [L,R=301]

A few notes:
- `RewriteRule` matches the URL path only, not the query string.
- `RewriteCond` checks the query string.
- The final `?` in the target strips the old query string from the redirect.

If you need to match the entire long query exactly, you can, but it’s usually easier to match only the key part you care about.

To add your www domain in Google Webmaster Tools, first make sure `www.yourdomain.com` points to the correct site in GoDaddy DNS (for example, to `ghs.google.com` if you’re using Google Sites).

If you also want `yourdomain.com` to go to `www.yourdomain.com`, that is not handled by DNS. You need to set up domain forwarding/redirecting in GoDaddy.

GoDaddy provides free forwarding:
https://ph.godaddy.com/help/forward-a-domain-12123

After the www version is working and the redirect is set, add `www.yourdomain.com` as a property in Google Webmaster Tools.

Yes. If you want all requests on `www.somesite.com` to go to the same path on `www.someothersite.com`, add this to the old site’s `.htaccess` in the web root:

`Redirect 301 / http://www.someothersite.com/`

This will permanently redirect all URLs and preserve the rest of the path/query string.

Note: if WordPress rewrite rules are already in that `.htaccess`, they may run first. In that case, disable/comment out the existing `RewriteRule` entries or put the redirect before them so the redirect happens.

To make it a 301 redirect, the target must be a full absolute URL, not a local path.

Example:

RewriteRule ^(\S+)/directory/(\d+)/(\d+)/entry/(\d+)/?$ http://www.example.com/directories/index.cfm?sFuseAction=XXX.YYYY.ZZZZ&nDirectoryID=$2&nEntryID=$4&nCategoryID=$3&sDirectory=$1 [NC,L,R=301]

Notes:
- Add `R=301` to force the redirect.
- Use your real domain and protocol.
- If the old URL includes `surveys/`, match it in the pattern too if needed.

A 500 from .htaccess usually means Apache is rejecting one of the directives, not the redirect itself.

Try this minimal version first:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.blog.mysite.co.uk/$1 [R=301,L]

If that works, the problem is likely:

- `Options +FollowSymLinks` not allowed by server config
- `mod_rewrite` not enabled
- `AllowOverride` restrictions in Apache

Also, if you’re redirecting an entire subdomain to another site, a simpler setup may be better done in the virtual host config or DNS/web server config, not .htaccess.

Use a 301 redirect from the old username URL to the new one.

A 301 says the resource has permanently moved, which is the right signal for a username change and helps preserve link equity. It does not prevent that old URL from being reused later. If a different user later claims the old username, you can simply stop redirecting that URL and serve the new content with a 200 response.

Search engines will recrawl the URL when they find new links or sitemap entries, and once they see the 200 response again, they can reindex it.

Best for SEO is usually:

1. Keep the old domain live for a while.
2. 301 redirect each old URL to the most relevant new URL, page by page.
3. Also update internal links, sitemap, canonicals, and submit the new site in Google Search Console.

Avoid redirecting everything only to the new homepage unless there’s no equivalent page. That causes a poor user experience and loses relevance signals.

Don’t keep both sites competing long-term. The old site should mainly act as a permanent redirect source.

If possible:
- one-to-one redirects for matching content
- homepage to homepage
- old pages with no match to the closest relevant page, or a category page
- verify both domains in Search Console and use the Change of Address tool if moving domains

This is better than just adding backlinks from the old site.

Yes — in GoDaddy, “Forward only” with Redirect type set to “301 (Permanent)” is the search-engine-friendly 301 redirect you want.

“Forward with masking” is different; it uses a frame and is not a true 301 redirect.

So, to do a real 301:
- Choose Redirect type: 301 (Permanent)
- Choose Forward settings: Forward only

That should be sufficient.

If you’re redirecting users from an old site to a new one, use proper 301 redirects for every old URL to its closest new URL. This preserves SEO value and sends search engines and users to the right place.

Best practices:
- Keep the same domain if possible; if not, map old pages one-to-one.
- Use 301, not 302, for permanent moves.
- Update internal links, canonical tags, sitemap, and hreflang.
- Set up Google Search Console for the new site and submit the new sitemap.
- Make sure the old site stays live with redirects for months, not days.

If you mean “how to tell users about the new site,” use email, social media, and announcements too—don’t rely only on search engines.

GoDaddy’s “redirect with masking” isn’t a true 301 pass-through. It loads the destination inside a frame/iframe, so the browser stays on your GoDaddy URL and the path of the page you click to won’t appear in the address bar.

That’s why the URL doesn’t change when you navigate.

If you want the actual page/file names to show in the URL, you need one of these:
- a real server-side redirect from your own host
- domain forwarding without masking
- hosting the site on the domain itself and linking normally

If you want, I can show you how to verify the frame behavior in the page source.

For tech/scale/admin reasons, folders are usually simpler and easier to maintain.

If you want the “subdomain” look, you can often fake it with URL rewriting, like `client.myservice.com` mapping to `myservice.com/client/`, without the extra DNS/server complexity.

Use real subdomains mainly when:
- they point to separate servers/services, or
- each customer/site is effectively its own isolated app.

So in most cases, choose sub-directories unless you have a strong architectural reason to isolate them.

For most SEO cases, choose a sub-directory if the content is part of the same site.

Why:
- A sub-folder shares the main domain’s authority more directly.
- It’s usually easier to track, manage, and consolidate SEO signals.
- Search engines can still crawl either, but subfolders are often simpler for site structure.

Use a sub-domain if:
- The content is a clearly separate product/brand/team.
- You need a different technical setup or independent hosting.
- You want separate branding and administration.

So if “company” is just a section of the main site, use:
www.mysite.com/company

If it’s more like a separate site, use:
company.mysite.com

If you want, I can also explain the SEO tradeoffs in more detail.

If you have the choice, use sub-directories rather than sub-domains for this setup.

Why:
- You already have unlimited addon domains, but they can only map to `/`, so sub-directories fit your hosting limits better.
- With `.htaccess`, you can rewrite each domain to its own folder and keep the folder hidden from users.
- SEO-wise, either can work, but sub-directories are usually simpler to manage when everything is on the same site/account.

For your case, the resolved thread shows this approach works:
- rewrite `site1.com` to `/site1/`
- rewrite `site2.com` to `/site2/`
- add a rule to force trailing slashes so `/test` becomes `/test/` before rewriting

So yes: sub-directories are the practical choice here.

Use both.

A 301 redirect from `page.php` to `page` is the primary fix: it sends users and Google to the preferred URL and consolidates link equity. Add a rel="canonical" tag on the final page pointing to `page` as an extra signal.

Best practice:
- Keep only one public URL per page
- 301 redirect all `*.php` URLs to the clean URL
- Use canonical on the destination page

If you can only choose one, choose the 301 redirect. Canonical helps, but it’s weaker than a redirect.

If Google is indexing the PHP files because they’re under `/content/`, then blocking that directory in `robots.txt` will stop Google from crawling those PHP URLs, but it can also block any real pages that live under `/content/`.

So:
- If `/content/` contains only junk or non-public files, add:
  Disallow: /content/
- If important pages are inside `/content/`, don’t block the whole folder.

Google crawls by following links, so if it sees URLs like `/content/foo/bar.php`, it may also try `/content/foo` and `/content/`.

Keywords in URLs can help a little, but only marginally. They may make links easier for users to understand and can provide a tiny SEO signal, but they’re far less important than page content, title tags, headings, and link text.

So:
- Good: readable, natural URLs with a relevant keyword or two
- Not necessary: forcing keywords into every URL
- Avoid: changing an existing URL structure just for SEO unless there’s a strong reason

In short, they’re not redundant, but they’re also not a major ranking factor. Focus on clarity and usability first.

No — Google’s removal tool doesn’t support wildcard de-indexing like `file.php*`.

If those URLs should no longer exist, the best fix is to make them return a proper `410 Gone` (or `404 Not Found`) so Google drops them naturally on recrawl. If they’ve just moved or have alternate versions, use `301` redirects and canonical tags to point Google to the preferred URL.

If you want, I can also suggest the quickest way to handle 10,000 parameterized PHP URLs in bulk.

Repeating the thread title in a forum is usually not keyword stuffing by itself.

Google understands forum pages and expects some repetition because the title appears in the meta title, H3, thread title, and in replies. What matters is whether the page reads naturally and the keywords are used in context. If the page is full of repeated phrases with little real content, that can look spammy.

So:
- Natural repetition in titles/headers/posts: fine
- Excessive, unnatural repetition just to rank: risky

In your case, 30–70 repeats on a busy forum page is not automatically a problem if the content is normal and helpful.

No. Google Authorship via `rel="author"` is no longer supported.

Google stopped using it and now prefers structured data/schema markup for authorship and other rich results. So adding multiple `rel="author"` links won’t help with Google.

You can still use `rel="author"` as a general microformat for other tools/apps, but for Google, use structured data and clear bylines/citations instead.

Yes—using the same “ratings-reviews-prices” suffix on every product URL would likely look spammy/keyword-stuffed, especially if it’s repeated sitewide without variation.

It’s better to keep URLs short and descriptive, e.g.:
`example.com/unique-product-name`

Then make sure the page itself naturally includes pricing, ratings, and reviews if those are relevant. Google can understand those signals from the page content, title tag, headings, and structured data without forcing them into every URL.

In short: don’t stuff the URL; use clean, unique slugs and put the keywords where they fit naturally.

Keywords in the URL are not automatically “stuffing.” If the URL reflects a real, useful category/filter page with enough distinct content, that’s generally fine.

Key points:
- Google treats keywords in the path and in query strings similarly.
- What matters more is whether each URL represents a meaningful, indexable page or just thin/duplicate generated content.
- Using query strings instead of rewriting does not inherently reduce risk.
- Don’t overload the URL with lots of terms just for SEO; 3–4 descriptive words is usually enough.

So: use descriptive URLs for usability and clarity, but avoid cramming every possible filter into the URL.

Yes—Google can see multiple `rel="author"` links, but the important thing is that the author relationship should be clear and not ambiguous.

A few key points:

- `rel="author"` is an HTML5 link relation, so it does not require a Google Profile to be valid.
- For Google authorship features, they historically preferred a connection to a Google Profile to show a photo or rich result.
- `rel="me"` is for asserting identity across sites, and can be used alongside author markup.
- If you have multiple author links on a page, Google may ignore them if they create confusion.

Best practice: use one clear author link per page/article, and if possible use schema.org author markup too.

Google’s authorship markup was intended for people, not brands or multiple authors per page. In practice, you can mark up multiple authors, but Google has not clearly supported displaying multiple rel="author" links as one authorship result.

So:

- Multiple rel="author" links are technically possible.
- Google may ignore them, pick one, or not show authorship at all.
- For non-article/product pages, authorship was especially outside the intended scope.

If you’re trying this for SEO, don’t rely on multiple author links for ranking or rich snippets. Use more standard structured data instead.

Google PageRank is old and not a useful indicator of current ranking or traffic.

A few key points:
- PageRank is calculated per page, not per site.
- The visible PR number was always stale, just a snapshot of past data.
- Google updates internal PageRank far more often than the public toolbar ever did.
- An increase of 1 PR point is unlikely to explain a 300% traffic jump.

Your traffic increase was more likely caused by:
- new backlinks
- ranking changes for specific keywords
- content changes
- seasonal/search demand shifts

So PR is more of a reflection of past authority, not the direct cause of the traffic change.

Google doesn’t provide a PageRank history for exact sites/pages. The only PageRank data ever exposed publicly was a periodic snapshot, such as the old Toolbar PR, and Google stopped updating that long ago. For pages created after the last data refresh, you may see n/a because no newer PR data was released.

If you need history, you would have had to record it yourself over time.

Rather than relying on PageRank, check:
- whether Googlebot crawls the page
- whether the page is indexed
- whether it ranks for target keywords
- whether it gets search referrals

These are much more useful signals than stale PR data.

Generally, yes — category pages can be useful for search engines if they add value for users. They help search engines understand your site structure and can rank for broader topic queries.

But if your category/tag pages are thin, duplicate, or often rank above the actual article when that’s not desirable, using noindex on them can be a good idea.

Key point from the resolved thread: Google doesn’t recommend blocking duplicate pages via robots.txt just to avoid indexing. If you want them crawled but not indexed, use noindex in the page/template headers, not robots.txt.

So:
- Good to index: useful, unique category pages
- Better to noindex: low-value, duplicate, or misleading listing pages

Generally, category pages can be good to index if they’re useful landing pages and have unique, helpful content. But thin, duplicated archive pages often don’t add much value and can dilute crawl budget.

From the resolved thread you shared: one case found that noindexing WordPress tag/category archives plus improving pagination increased traffic by 30% in two weeks. So if your category pages are mostly lists with little original content, noindexing them is often a good choice.

Best practice:
- Index them if they are rich, well-written, and user-focused.
- Noindex them if they’re thin, repetitive, or low-value.

If you want, I can help you decide for your site specifically.

Usually, no—not if the category pages are thin, duplicate, or exist only to increase indexed pages.

Search engines prefer useful, unique pages. If a category page helps visitors discover content, has clear organization, and contains substantial text or listings, it can be worth indexing. If it’s just a page made for SEO, it may hurt more than help.

Best practice:
- Index useful category pages
- Noindex low-value or empty categories
- Avoid pages created only to boost count

Put users first and search engines second. If the page is genuinely helpful, index it; if not, exclude it.

Using hierarchical link relationships like rel="index", rel="start", rel="prev", and rel="next" can help search engines and browsers understand how pages relate to each other, but the SEO impact is usually small. It’s not a major ranking factor by itself.

It can still be worth doing because:
- it improves document structure
- it helps users navigate related pages
- it may assist search engines in discovering and grouping content

For SEO, the bigger wins are:
- clear site architecture
- internal linking
- good titles/meta
- quality content
- crawlable URLs

So yes, it’s good practice, but don’t expect a big rank boost from it alone.

Yes—hierarchical, crawlable site links generally help SEO more than a sitemap alone.

A sitemap helps search engines discover URLs, but actual links on pages are stronger because they show site structure and help crawlers move through your content. If your main navigation is a search form, adding a browseable hierarchy can still be useful, especially if it’s meant for users too.

Best practices:
- Use real HTML links, not just JS or form actions.
- Add breadcrumbs where possible.
- Keep the hierarchy logical and shallow.
- Don’t make it only for spiders; make it useful for visitors too.

For 5 million pages, a sitemap is still important, but it should complement crawlable internal links, not replace them.

A big navigation menu is not automatically bad for SEO. What matters most is whether the link structure helps Google understand your site hierarchy.

From the resolved thread: the issue was not “too many links” by itself, but that lower-level links were being treated like separate, equal pages and that diluted topical focus.

Best practice:
- Keep top-level navigation prominent and crawlable.
- Use a clear URL hierarchy, e.g. /category/subcategory/product/.
- Don’t surface every deep link on every page if it weakens site structure.
- Use content silos/internal linking to reinforce themes.

Hiding links only with hover or CSS is not a reliable SEO fix. If you want deep links visible to users but less prominent for SEO, use JavaScript-driven menus carefully and focus on strong hierarchy.

Hyphens are generally better for SEO when you’re separating words in a URL slug, because search engines can read them as word separators.

Slashes are fine for representing site structure or hierarchy, like:
`/products/shoes/running/`

Best practice:
- Use slashes to show folders/categories
- Use hyphens inside a page name: `/running-shoes/`
- Keep URLs short, clear, and meaningful

So it’s not really “slash vs hyphen” globally — use both appropriately. Avoid unnecessary deep nesting, but slash depth itself isn’t usually a direct SEO penalty.

For SEO, use hyphens in URLs/path names, not slashes to join words.

- **Hyphens (`-`)** are the standard way to separate words in a page URL: `example.com/seo-tips`
- **Slashes (`/`)** are for separating sections or folders: `example.com/seo/tips`

So:
- Good: `example.com/stack-overflow`
- Not for word separation: `example.com/stack/overflow` unless those are truly different sections

For **domain names**, avoid hyphens if possible, since they’re harder to say, type, and remember.

Article submission directories can provide backlinks, but their SEO value is generally low and has declined over time. Search engines have reduced trust in mass-submitted, duplicate content on article directories, especially after updates targeting content farms.

They may help a little for very uncompetitive keywords, but for most cases they’re not worth much compared with:
- guest posting on reputable sites
- earning links from relevant, authoritative sources
- creating content that attracts organic mentions

So: useful only marginally, and usually not the best use of time if your goal is lasting SEO gains.

Yes—if you can’t identify the bot by user agent and only by IP, the practical way is to rate-limit that IP at the web server or firewall level.

On Apache, you can ask your host to use request-throttling modules or similar controls. The referenced approach is to limit requests/traffic per IP, which effectively “slows down” a crawler instead of blocking it.

See:
https://serverfault.com/questions/131364/apache-limit-the-number-of-requests-traffic-per-ip

If you share your hosting setup, I can suggest the exact Apache/.htaccess or module-based rule to request from your provider.

Article submission directories can provide a small SEO benefit, mainly by creating backlinks to your site. However, their value is usually minimal because most directories rank poorly and have little authority.

In practice:
- They may help a bit for niche topics or low-competition keywords.
- For broad, competitive searches, they rarely make a meaningful difference.
- The links are generally weak, so results are slow and limited.

If you use them, focus on reputable, relevant directories rather than mass-submitting everywhere. For finding directories, “directories of directories” like directorycritic.com can help.

If Googlebot crawl rate feels too slow on a huge site, first verify whether the traffic is really Googlebot.

A “Googlebot” User-Agent is easy to spoof. Check the source IPs and confirm they resolve to Google-owned ranges / validate via reverse DNS and forward DNS. If the IPs aren’t Google, it’s likely spoofed traffic, not real crawl.

If it is real Googlebot and crawl is still too slow:
- make sure the site is fast and returns consistent 200s
- submit/refresh an XML sitemap
- improve internal linking to important pages
- avoid crawl traps, duplicate URLs, and long redirect chains
- check Search Console crawl stats and index coverage
- don’t block key resources in robots.txt

If you want, I can help you verify whether your logs contain real Googlebot IPs.

Linkbaiting is creating content, features, or headlines specifically designed to attract links from other websites. In SEO, it usually means making something highly shareable or useful so others naturally link to it.

It can be:
- a useful guide or tool
- a controversial or catchy article
- an infographic or data study
- a funny or surprising piece of content

Done well, linkbait earns backlinks and traffic. Done badly, it can feel manipulative or clickbait-like if the content doesn’t deliver value.

In short: content made to “bait” other sites into linking to it.

Use a subdomain for it.

`www.subdomain.domain.com` is just another subdomain level, so you need to create a DNS record for `www.subdomain` — not just `www`.

In GoDaddy, add a CNAME like:

`www.subdomain -> subdomain.domain.com`

or point it wherever your host requires.

If you want it managed in GoDaddy, use the Hosted Domains / Add Subdomain option in the control panel. The key is that `www.subdomain` must exist as its own DNS entry.

Link baiting is creating content specifically designed to attract backlinks from other websites. The “bait” is usually something highly useful, surprising, entertaining, or controversial that people want to reference and share.

Common examples:
- Original research or statistics
- Free tools or templates
- Strong opinions or controversial posts
- Infographics, guides, or how-tos
- Funny or highly shareable content

In SEO, it can be very useful because natural backlinks can improve authority and rankings. The key is to make content genuinely valuable, not just promotional or clickbait. Good link bait solves a problem or gives people a reason to link to it.

A domain is the main website name, like example.com.

A subdomain is a prefix added in front, like blog.example.com or shop.example.com.

Use a subdomain when you want a separate section or service under the same main domain. It can help organize content, run different apps, or separate environments like dev.example.com.

Use the main domain when you want everything under one site.

For SEO, subdomains can sometimes be treated a bit separately from the main domain, while subfolders like example.com/blog are often easier to manage together.

If you’re a beginner, start with the main domain unless you have a clear reason to split things into subdomains.

Register the custom domain (`domain.com`) in Google Webmaster Tools.

Why:
- It’s the domain you control.
- It will remain valid even if you later move away from WordPress.com.
- The WordPress subdomain (`domain.wordpress.com`) is controlled by WordPress and may stop being your main site.

If you’re only using WordPress.com’s custom domain mapping for now, either can work. But as a general rule, `domain.com` is the better choice.

If you want the browser to keep showing `sub.domain.com` while content comes from another server, you need a reverse proxy, not a redirect.

A normal redirect sends the user to `sub.domain.org`, so the URL changes.

Typical Apache reverse proxy setup:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
  ServerName sub.domain.com
  ProxyPreserveHost On
  ProxyPass / http://domain.org/
  ProxyPassReverse / http://domain.org/
</VirtualHost>
```

This makes `sub.domain.com` act as a front end for `domain.org`.

An iframe can also display the other site, but it’s usually a worse solution and can cause SEO/SSL issues.

For items under sections/categories, the best architecture is usually:

- Create a main category page that can rank and is easy to navigate.
- Break large lists into paginated subpages for crawlability and tracking.
- Also add anchor links/toc links within the main page for quick jumps to sections.
- If you offer a “view all” page, set a canonical to the preferred version to avoid duplicate-content issues.
- Don’t expect Google to index section anchors as separate URLs unless they have their own distinct URL.

Good pattern:
/category/
/category/page/2/
/category/section/top-rated/ or #top-rated for jumping within page

If you want SEO plus UX, use real subcategory URLs for important sections, and anchors only for in-page navigation.

Yes, you can rank for a non-English keyword on an English site if that term appears on the page and the page is relevant.

But adding translated Spanish/French content should not, by itself, hurt your English rankings. Google ranks pages using many factors, and keyword lists in Webmaster Tools/Search Console are just crawl counts, not a direct ranking signal.

If the foreign-language content is mixed into the English pages, it can confuse indexing. Best practice is to separate languages clearly:
- use dedicated language URLs
- add hreflang
- avoid mixing languages on the same page when possible

If you want, I can help you check whether your site structure is causing the ranking drop.

Spanish text on an English page can confuse Google about the page’s language/topic, especially if it’s prominent near the top or in links. That can affect sitelinks and may make Google less confident about which language version to show, but it usually won’t “penalize” the page by itself.

Best practice:
- Keep each language on its own URL/folder.
- Make the page language consistent.
- Put language-switch links in the footer, not near the top.
- Use hreflang and register both language sections in Search Console.
- Remove or reduce mixed-language navigation on the English page.

If the Spanish text is just at the bottom and not central, impact is usually small.

A few Spanish words at the bottom of an otherwise English page usually won’t make the page rank for Spanish keywords. Search engines look at the overall language and relevance of the page, not just a small snippet.

If the main content is English, the page will generally be treated as English. But mixing languages can hurt user experience and make the page look less focused, which may slightly reduce relevance signals.

Best practice:
- Keep each page in one language
- Use separate URLs/domains or subfolders for each language
- Add hreflang tags
- Avoid mixed-language content unless it’s intentional

If you want, I can explain how bilingual pages should be structured for SEO.

A small amount of Spanish text at the bottom of an otherwise English page can make Google see the page as somewhat bilingual or partially Spanish. That can:

- help a little for Spanish queries if the Spanish text is meaningful
- slightly dilute the English signal if the Spanish text is substantial

If it’s just a short footer note or disclaimer, the impact is usually minimal. But if your goal is to rank primarily for English terms, keep the main content, title, URL, and metadata in English, and avoid adding unnecessary Spanish text. Google mostly uses the dominant language on the page, not a small block at the bottom.

Not really. Google can’t be told to ignore just certain words on a page while still indexing the rest of that same page.

If a page is public and contains “unicorn,” it may be matched for that term. Your options are:

- remove or rewrite the unwanted content
- split the content onto a different page
- block the page or section entirely with robots.txt / noindex if you don’t want it indexed
- keep the “unicorn” content in a private area

So if you want the page found for “strawberry” but not “unicorn,” the practical fix is to avoid publishing “unicorn” on that public page.

To tell Google to ignore parts of a website, use a robots.txt file on the part you want excluded.

For your example, place a robots.txt in the root of the static subdomain, such as:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

That tells crawlers like Googlebot not to crawl anything on that subdomain.

Notes:
- robots.txt blocks crawling, not necessarily indexing if other sites link to it.
- If you need stronger removal, use password protection or noindex tags where possible.

More info: http://www.robotstxt.org/robotstxt.html

If you want a free, user-friendly alternative to reCAPTCHA, try a honeypot field.

How it works:
- Add an extra input field to your form
- Hide it with JavaScript
- On the server, reject submissions if that field is filled in

Why it helps:
- Real users won’t see it
- Many bots will fill it automatically
- Much less annoying than CAPTCHA

You can also combine it with:
- rate limiting
- form timing checks
- server-side validation

For many forms, a honeypot alone works very well.

- memberlist.php
- viewtopic.php
- viewforum.php
- ucp.php
- viewonline.php

- reCAPTCHA/hCaptcha on registration
- email confirmation
- banning disposable email domains
- rate limiting / firewall rules
- anti-bot plugins for phpBB

If you want to grow visibility without spam, focus on promotion and community building:

- Publish useful content regularly
- Share updates on relevant social channels
- Submit press releases when there’s real news
- Participate in related forums/communities
- Encourage discussions, comments, or a newsletter
- Build partnerships and get legitimate backlinks

Avoid mass posting, keyword stuffing, or unsolicited messages. Those can hurt your reputation and SEO.

To cut spam while keeping both a visible email and a contact form:

- Obfuscate the email address so bots can’t easily harvest it:
  - render it with JavaScript after page load
  - encode it in the HTML
  - or display it as an image

- Protect the contact form with anti-spam checks:
  - CAPTCHA
  - honeypot field
  - rate limiting / throttling
  - server-side validation

Also make sure form submissions are filtered before they reach your inbox. No single method stops all spam, but combining these usually removes most of it.

A good, user-friendly alternative to reCAPTCHA is a honeypot field.

How it works:
- Add a hidden input field to your form
- Leave it invisible with JavaScript
- On the server, reject submissions if that field is filled in

Why it helps:
- Humans won’t see it
- Many bots won’t parse the JS to detect it
- It’s much less intrusive than CAPTCHAs

Also consider combining it with:
- server-side rate limiting
- email verification
- form submission timing checks

For many cases, a honeypot plus rate limiting is a very effective setup.

Use a single redirect that checks both host and HTTPS:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !on
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://www.example.com/$1 [R=301,L]
```

This sends:

- `http://example.com` → `https://www.example.com`
- `https://example.com` → `https://www.example.com`
- `http://www.example.com` → `https://www.example.com`

If you also have other subdomains, keep the host check specific to `example.com` only.

A good low-friction way is to use a honeypot field in your forms.

Add an extra field that real users won’t see, then reject submissions if it has any value. Example:

```html
<input type="text" name="email" id="mailfield">
```

```css
#mailfield { display: none; }
```

If the hidden field is filled in, it’s likely a bot, so you can discard the submission.

This won’t stop every spammer, but it blocks a lot of automated junk without annoying users. For stronger protection, combine it with CAPTCHA, rate limiting, and server-side validation.

If you control the site, the best defense is layered:

- Keep server-side validation and CAPTCHAs, but don’t rely on them alone.
- Add a minimum time-on-page check before the form can be submitted; this helps against manual copy/paste spam.
- Use a honeypot field hidden from real users but visible to bots.
- Rate-limit submissions per IP, subnet, and email address.
- Require email verification or logged-in users for higher-risk forms.
- Block obvious abuse patterns and automate moderation/blacklists where possible.

For spam that’s manually entered by people, no solution is perfect; slowing submissions down and increasing cost is usually most effective.

If you control the site, the main defenses are:

- **Validate the Host header** on your server and only serve your real domains; reject or redirect unknown hosts.
- **Use virtual host rules** to map only approved domains.
- **Return a 403/404** for unrecognized domains instead of your content.
- **Add canonical tags** so search engines know the preferred URL.
- **Set up rate limiting / CAPTCHA / moderation** on forms and user-generated content to stop comment or signup spam.

If the spammer is pointing another domain at your IP, you usually can’t stop them from doing that, but you can prevent them from displaying your content by rejecting unknown hostnames. Contact your hosting provider if you need network-level help.

No — in your robots.txt, only Baiduspider is blocked by:

User-agent: Baiduspider
Disallow: /

That means Baiduspider should not crawl your site.

The other rule:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /templates_c/

applies to all other search engines, but only blocks the /templates_c/ directory, not the whole site.

If you had:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

then yes, that would block the entire site for all crawlers.

404.7 (FILE_EXTENSION_DENIED) usually means IIS Request Filtering is blocking the extension at a more specific scope than you expect.

Check these in IIS Manager:
- Select the affected site/application/folder
- Open Request Filtering
- Under File Name Extensions, confirm .html/.htm are allowed
- Also check Hidden Segments and HTTP Verbs tabs

Common cause: a setting at the folder/app level overrides the server/site level. If one folder works and another doesn’t, compare their requestFiltering settings and any inherited web.config entries. If needed, add an allow rule for the specific directory or remove a deny rule.

If your old pages were only blocked by robots.txt, Google may still keep them indexed. Robots blocking prevents crawling, not de-indexing.

- Set up 301 redirects from each old URL to the new URL.
- Keep the new pages crawlable and indexable.
- Use Google Search Console to inspect coverage and request indexing.
- If a page should be removed, return 404/410 or use a proper noindex method that Google can crawl.

Also, if other sites still link to the old URLs, redirects help Google understand the move and pass signals to the new pages.

So: don’t rely on robots.txt alone for duplicates; use 301 redirects.

Practical takeaway:
- Don’t panic over random spam links.
- Monitor backlinks and Search Console.
- If you see obvious attack patterns, document them and disavow only when necessary.
- Focus on strong content, technical SEO, and natural links.

If you want Google to crawl a page but not show it in results, use:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow" />

That lets Google read the page and follow its links, while keeping it out of search results.

Check your sitemap URLs:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /store-o

Sitemap: http://www.proboxinggear.com/store/sitemaps.xml

After updating, resubmit the sitemap in Google Search Console and request indexing for important pages.

Yes. Google can discover a site even if no other site links to it, but it’s much less likely. If a page is truly unlinked, Google may still find it through:

Best practice:
- Back up everything first.
- Test on a dev/staging site, ideally on the same server or a subdomain.

- If you must switch hosts, minimize downtime and monitor Search Console.

Usually, moving images to a CDN does not hurt Google Image indexing by itself. Google can index images from a CDN URL just fine.

What matters more is:
- alt text
- surrounding page content
- image filename
- whether the image is still crawlable

If your images were helping rankings before, changing the URL can temporarily affect signals, but using a CNAME on your own domain is a good way to keep the URL consistent and reduce risk.

Moving images to a CDN should not inherently hurt Google Image Search results. Google can still index and show CDN-hosted images.

What can change is how Google fetches and caches the image preview:
- Google may show its own thumbnail from `gstatic` instead of your live image.
- If the CDN blocks hotlinking, redirects, or serves inconsistent headers, Google may keep using the cached thumbnail.
- A URL change can also make Google treat it as a new image, which can temporarily affect rankings.

Best practices:
- Keep image URLs stable
- Allow Googlebot/image fetches from the CDN
- Return a direct image response, not a redirect to HTML
- Use proper `Content-Type` and cache headers

So: CDN migration itself is usually fine; access/redirect/caching behavior is what matters.

- Keep the site reliably up 24/7
- Make sure all old URLs return 200 OK and content matches what used to be there
- Update or add new content regularly
- Resubmit your sitemap in Google Search Console
- Check for crawl errors, broken links, and server issues
- Rebuild links from sites that used to point to you

In practice, trust tends to return over a few months if the site stays stable and useful.

- submit the sitemap in Search Console
- fetch/crawl key pages to speed reindexing
- check for broken links, noindex tags, and robots.txt blocks

The earlier thread applies to temporary maintenance: use 503, and include Retry-After if possible. For a 6-month outage, just restore the site and let crawlers recrawl it.

Yes—multiple redirects can have a small negative SEO impact. Google has said some trust/authority can be lost with each 301 hop, so a single 301 from old URL to new URL is best.

If your setup is:
old URL -> 301 -> another URL -> 301 -> final URL

that’s less ideal than a direct one-to-one redirect:
old URL -> 301 -> final URL

A two-step redirect usually won’t cause major problems, but avoid chains if you can. Also verify the final response with a header checker (e.g., Live HTTP Headers, HttpFox) to make sure only one 301 is happening.

A 301 from a spammy, low-PageRank site can pass signals to the target site, including potentially negative ones. So yes, it can hurt or at least create risk for the higher-ranking site.

If your goal is only to send human visitors to the new site, the safer options are:

- Don’t 301 the whole domain.
- Show a shutdown/notice page with a link to the new site.

If the old site has a bad link profile, it’s usually better to let it die or keep it as a simple notice page rather than merge it into the strong site.

Redirection itself usually isn’t the issue. If the comparison site uses tracking/redirect URLs, Google generally understands that these are paid or affiliate-style links, so they typically won’t pass ranking value (“juice”) like a normal editorial backlink would.

SEO-wise:
- You usually won’t get a ranking boost from those redirected links.
- It’s unlikely to hurt your rankings just because the links go through redirects.
- Google may still crawl and evaluate the page, but paid/tracked links are commonly treated as non-signaling for PageRank.

So: safe enough from an SEO risk perspective, but don’t expect direct ranking benefit from the links.

- Let Google recrawl it and show the newer date in results

So the benefit of a date in URL segments is mostly organizational, not SEO. A clean, permanent URL is generally better.

Using the date in the URL is mainly beneficial for permanence and sharing: each day’s page has a stable permalink, so users can bookmark and share it directly.

The main benefit of dates in URL segments is readability and hierarchy, not “search engine magic.”

`/date/2010/02/02` suggests a nested structure:
- year

That makes it easy to create related pages like:
- `/date/2010`
- `/date/2010/02`

By contrast, `date=2010-02-02` is better when the value is just a parameter in an unordered set.

So:
- use path segments for hierarchical, human-friendly resources
- use query parameters for filters, options, or non-hierarchical data

Search engines can understand both; the URL design is mostly about clarity and clean site structure.

4. Submit the new URL in Search Console and a sitemap.

- the naked domain 301-redirects to www

The best way is:

1. Add a `noindex` directive on the pages themselves, e.g.  
   `<meta name="googlebot" content="noindex">`

2. `robots.txt` alone is not enough — it only blocks crawling, not necessarily indexing.

If the directory is already indexed, also return `410 Gone` or `404` for those URLs and request removal in Google Search Console.

`site:example.com/your-directory/`
and check whether results still appear.

Use the web server, not DNS, for a true redirect. DNS can point `example.com` and `www.example.com` to the same IP, but it cannot issue an HTTP redirect.

If you’re on IIS, add a rewrite rule in `web.config` to redirect the naked domain to `www`:

```xml
<rewrite>
  <rules>
    <rule name="Redirect naked to www" stopProcessing="true">
      <match url=".*" />
      <conditions>
        <add input="{HTTP_HOST}" pattern="^example\.com$" />
      </conditions>
      <action type="Redirect" url="http://www.example.com/{R:1}" redirectType="Permanent" />
    </rule>
  </rules>
</rewrite>
```

Also make sure both hostnames point to the site in DNS/IIS bindings. If you want, I can give you the exact IIS steps.

Soft 404s in GWT usually mean Google thinks a URL returns a “page-like” response but the content is effectively missing or empty.

- Log request handling to see whether the URL rewrite is failing or generating a blank page.
- Verify the page renders meaningful content, not just header/footer with an empty body.
- If parameters shouldn’t create unique pages, canonicalize or ignore them properly.

In Google Search Console, “soft 404” usually means Google can fetch the URL, but the page looks like an error or thin/empty content page.

To fix it:

- Make sure missing pages return a real HTTP 404 or 410, not 200 OK.
- If the page exists, ensure it has substantial unique content, not just a placeholder, redirect page, or “not found” message.
- Check for browser-side redirects or JavaScript that hides content from Google.
- Verify canonical tags point to the correct live URL.
- Remove internal links to URLs that should not exist.
- Test the affected URL with Fetch as Google / URL Inspection.

- **Non-compliant bots** ignoring robots.txt
- **Referrals/bookmarks/email/social links**
- **Search results showing the URL without crawling the page**
- **Cached/old links** or pre-existing indexing

Even with `Disallow: /`, your site can still get traffic because robots.txt only tells well-behaved search engine crawlers not to crawl pages. It does not block:

- users visiting the site directly
- bots that ignore robots.txt
- already-indexed URLs appearing in search results
- cached/search-snippet visits
- links from other sites

If the old product is truly discontinued, don’t 301 it to a “very similar” product unless it’s effectively the same item. For SEO, a 301 tells search engines the old URL has permanently moved and passes signals to the new URL.

So: discontinued item -> 410; near-identical replacement -> 301.

If the page is permanently deleted and not replaced, the best SEO practice is to return **HTTP 410 Gone**. This clearly tells search engines the URL has been intentionally removed, so they can drop it faster than with a 404.

Avoid using **301 redirects** unless you have a truly relevant replacement page. Redirecting deleted content to the homepage or an unrelated page can confuse users and search engines.

For the response page, include a helpful message and links to:
- your homepage
- sitemap
- site search
- related/similar content, if available

If the content is only temporarily unavailable, use a different status code such as **404** or **503** depending on the situation.

When deleting a webpage, the main SEO goal is to tell search engines the page is gone and, if possible, where users should go instead.

Best practices:
- If there is a close replacement, use a 301 redirect to the most relevant page.
- If the page is permanently removed with no replacement, return 404 or 410.
  - 404 = not found
  - 410 = gone, and is a clearer signal that the removal is intentional
- Remove internal links to the deleted page.
- Update XML sitemaps and any canonical tags.
- If the page has backlinks or traffic, prefer redirecting rather than deleting.

Rule of thumb:
- Use 301 if there’s a new equivalent page.
- Use 410 if it’s permanently deleted and should drop from the index faster.
- Use 404 if you can’t or don’t want to explicitly signal permanent removal.

If your site is available on both HTTP and HTTPS, that can create duplicate content **if both versions are indexable** and there’s no clear preferred version.

What to do:
- Pick **HTTPS** as the canonical version
- 301 redirect all HTTP URLs to HTTPS
- Make sure internal links use HTTPS
- Add/verify `<link rel="canonical" href="https://...">`
- Check that both versions aren’t separately indexable in search engines

If HTTPS is the only accessible version, or HTTP properly redirects to it, duplicate content is usually **not** a problem.

To minimize duplicate-content SEO impact when forcing HTTPS site wide:

- Use **301 redirects** from every old HTTP URL to the matching HTTPS URL.
- **Do not block** the HTTP URLs in robots.txt; Google needs to crawl the redirect.
- Update **all internal links** to HTTPS.
- Regenerate your **XML sitemap** with HTTPS URLs only.
- Verify the HTTPS property in **Google Search Console** and submit the sitemap there.
- Keep the redirects in place long term so Google can fully replace old URLs in the index.

This lets Google consolidate ranking signals from HTTP to HTTPS and avoids duplicate-content problems.

When moving an existing site to HTTPS site-wide, the main goal is to make sure search engines see only one preferred version of each page.

Best practice:
- Pick HTTPS as the canonical version.
- 301 redirect all HTTP URLs to their HTTPS equivalents.
- Update internal links, sitemaps, canonicals, hreflang, and structured data to HTTPS.
- Set the HTTPS version in Google Search Console and submit the new sitemap.
- Avoid serving both HTTP and HTTPS without redirects, as that can look like duplicate content.

If both versions remain accessible, use rel="canonical" on the HTTP pages pointing to the HTTPS pages. This consolidates ranking signals and prevents duplicate-content SEO issues.

Enforcing HTTPS site-wide usually does not create duplicate-content SEO issues if you handle it correctly.

Best practice:

- manual action/penalty

Since Bing still ranks the site, it may be Google-specific. Check Google Search Console first:

5. Add a sitemap.xml so search engines can discover the URLs.
